title: Baseline Player Profile and Testing Orientation
objective: Develop a complete starting profile for each player by combining physical information, football background, positional role, self-assessment and coach observation before formal testing begins.
groundSize: Clubrooms, meeting area and a 20 × 20 metre football area.
equipment: Scales if body-mass recording is appropriate
setup:
Prepare one profile form for every player.
Divide the form into personal information, football background, preferred positions, current roles, injury considerations, goals and self-ratings.
Establish a short football activity area where coaches can observe basic movement, kicking, handballing and communication.
Explain that the profile is a starting point rather than a selection verdict.
Protect personal and medical information and restrict access to appropriate coaching or medical staff.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete the personal and football-background sections of the profile form.
Each player identifies preferred positions, previous positions, dominant side, secondary side and current role understanding.
Players rate their confidence in kicking, handballing, marking, ground-ball work, decision making, endurance, speed and communication.
Players record one short-term development goal and one longer-term football goal.
Coaches lead a five- to ten-minute low-intensity football activity and record initial observations.
The coach meets briefly with each player to clarify goals, injury considerations and role expectations.
Completed profiles are stored as the starting reference for future tests and reviews.
Testing categories are explained so players understand how later results will be used.
coachingPoints: Present profiling as a development tool rather than a judgement exercise.
Separate demonstrated performance from confidence and self-perception.
Record the player’s current role before suggesting a future role.
Ask clear questions and avoid leading the player towards a preferred answer.
Identify injury history or movement restrictions before physical testing.
Use consistent wording and rating scales across the squad.
Record observable behaviour rather than vague impressions.
Revisit player goals after testing rather than treating the first response as final.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player’s self-rating matches visible confidence and execution.
The player’s understanding of positional responsibilities.
Communication habits during the introductory football activity.
Differences between dominant-side and non-dominant-side confidence.
Whether the player can identify a specific development goal.
Players who may require additional explanation or modified testing.
progressions: Add individual player interviews with line coaches.
Compare player self-ratings with coach ratings after the first testing battery.
Add leadership, communication and training-behaviour ratings.
Link every player goal to one training action and one review date.
regressions: Use a shortened profile for younger players.
Complete the form through a coach-led conversation.
Use simple three-point ratings such as developing, capable and confident.
Remove body measurements where they are unnecessary or inappropriate.
Allow parents or guardians to assist younger players with background information.
successIndicators: Complete the profile honestly and with adequate detail.
Identify at least one meaningful development priority.
Understand the purpose of future testing.
Communicate relevant injury or movement restrictions.
Describe their preferred role and current role expectations.
Apply the same questions and rating scales to all players.
Use the profile to modify later testing where required.
matchApplication: A complete baseline profile helps coaches interpret football performance in context. Test results become more useful when they are connected to the player’s role, experience, physical condition, confidence and development goals rather than being viewed as isolated numbers.

title: Kicking Accuracy Baseline Test
objective: Measure each player’s current kicking accuracy from controlled and moving starts across short and medium distances using a repeatable testing method.
groundSize: A 40 × 30 metre area with marked kicking stations at 15, 25 and 35 metres.
setup:
Create three kicking stations at 15, 25 and 35 metres from a target gate.
Make the short target gate approximately 3 metres wide, the medium gate 4 metres wide and the long gate 5 metres wide.
Establish separate starting cones for stationary kicks and kicks after a five-metre approach.
Prepare a scoring system of two points for a kick through the gate, one point for a kick reaching the target player within one step, and zero points for an inaccurate or unmarkable kick.
Modify distances for younger or developing players while preserving the same scoring method.
Assign one recorder and one target player to each station where numbers allow.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each player completes two practice kicks at the first station.
The player then performs five scored kicks from 15 metres using the preferred foot.
The player performs five scored kicks from 15 metres using the non-preferred foot.
The same sequence is completed from 25 metres.
Suitable players complete five preferred-foot kicks and five non-preferred-foot kicks from 35 metres.
Players then repeat one five-kick set from 25 metres after receiving and moving through the approach cone.
Record the score, target side, kick type and any obvious technical breakdown.
Rotate players through kicking, targeting, football return and recording roles.
Calculate accuracy percentages for preferred foot, non-preferred foot, stationary kicking and kicking on the move.
coachingPoints: Use the same ball condition, distances and target widths for every tested player.
Do not provide technical coaching during the scored attempts.
Allow a standardised warm-up before testing.
Require the target player to remain in the same position.
Record whether misses are left, right, short or over the target.
Separate accuracy from distance capability.
Ensure the player begins each repetition from the marked starting point.
Retest under comparable conditions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The difference between preferred and non-preferred foot.
Whether movement before the kick improves or reduces accuracy.
Whether the player sacrifices control when attempting greater distance.
progressions: Add kicks after a ground-ball collection.
Add a time limit from possession to disposal.
Add position-specific kicks such as inside-50 entries, defensive exits or corridor passes.
Conduct a separate pressure-kicking test after the baseline has been established.
regressions: Test only the preferred foot initially.
Allow a stationary ball-drop rehearsal before each attempt.
Reduce the number of scored kicks for younger players.
successIndicators: Complete the required attempts using the same routine.
Produce accurate, markable kicks at age-appropriate distances.
Show a clear and repeatable miss pattern that can guide future coaching.
matchApplication: Accurate kicking is central to retaining possession, changing angles, entering the forward line and exiting defence. The test identifies the distances, sides and movement conditions under which each player can currently execute a reliable match disposal.

title: Decision-Making Observation Grid
objective: Assess how consistently players scan, recognise available options, select appropriate disposals and respond after possession changes during a controlled small-sided game.
groundSize: A 45 × 35 metre rectangle divided into three horizontal zones.
equipment: Two scoring gates at each end
setup:
Create two even teams.
Divide the playing area into defensive, midfield and attacking zones.
Place two scoring gates at each end to provide multiple attacking options.
Use normal football disposal rules with controlled pressure and no tackling to ground.
Assign one observer to a small group of players where staffing allows.
Prepare a five-category observation grid covering scanning, option choice, execution, support and turnover response.
Use a rating scale of one to five for each category.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play four-minute games with one minute between periods.
The team in possession attempts to move the football through either scoring gate.
Players may kick or handball and are encouraged to use available width.
After a turnover, both teams immediately change roles.
Observers track assigned players rather than following only the football.
For each involvement, record whether the player scanned before possession, selected an appropriate option, executed effectively, moved again and reacted after turnover.
At the end of each period, observers finalise ratings without discussing scores.
Players rotate positions between periods.
Complete at least three periods to avoid judging a player from one involvement.
Compare observations after all independent ratings are recorded.
coachingPoints: Observe behaviour before the player receives the football.
Rate the quality of the decision separately from execution.
Consider the information available at the moment of possession.
Avoid penalising an appropriate option solely because a teammate made an error.
Track off-ball support and turnover reaction.
Use repeated observations rather than one memorable action.
Keep constraints simple enough that genuine decisions remain available.
Do not coach individual decisions during the scored assessment periods.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Recognition of free teammates and dangerous space.
Whether the player selects kick, handball or carry appropriately.
Speed and confidence of the decision.
progressions: Add full tackling for suitable groups.
Compare decisions under fresh and fatigued conditions.
Use video review to confirm live observations.
regressions: Use an overload for the team in possession.
Remove tackling and restrict defenders to intercepts.
Reduce the observation grid to three categories.
Allow a coach pause between possessions for younger players.
successIndicators: Select options suited to pressure and field position.
Separate decision quality from execution quality.
Support ratings with repeated observable examples.
matchApplication: Football decisions occur before, during and after possession. This assessment identifies whether players recognise space, pressure, teammate position, field location and turnover consequences rather than measuring skill execution in isolation.

title: Player Testing Data Record and Benchmark System
objective: Establish a consistent system for recording, checking, interpreting and reviewing player testing results across a season.
players: Minimum: 1 Ideal: Full Squad Maximum: Multiple Squads
groundSize: Clubrooms, office or meeting area.
time: 30–60 minutes for initial setup; 10–20 minutes after each testing session
setup:
Create one record for every player.
Include player name, age group, date, test version, conditions, result, validity status and coach comments.
Separate raw scores from calculated scores.
Define how missed tests, modified tests and invalid attempts will be recorded.
Establish age-, role- or squad-specific benchmark groups.
Restrict access to approved staff.
Create a backup and version-control process.
howTheDrillWorks:
Enter each player’s identifying information and profile reference.
Record the exact test version and date.
Enter raw results before calculating percentages, averages or rankings.
Mark every result as valid, modified, incomplete or invalid.
Add relevant testing conditions such as wet footballs, wind, surface condition or player restriction.
Check entries against original recording sheets.
Calculate squad averages, ranges and position-group benchmarks.
Compare each player primarily with their own previous result before comparing them with others.
Flag meaningful improvement, decline or inconsistency for review.
Prepare a player-facing summary that uses clear language and limited, relevant measures.
Store the complete data securely for future retesting.
coachingPoints: Preserve raw data so calculations can be checked later.
Never combine results from different test versions without clearly identifying the difference.
Record modified tests separately from standard tests.
Use benchmarks to guide development rather than label players permanently.
Consider age, role, injury status and training history.
Check unusual results before drawing conclusions.
Avoid ranking players when the measure has weak match relevance.
Protect player privacy.
Use the same naming and coding system across every testing session.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Results entered under the wrong player or date.
Sudden changes that may indicate data-entry error.
Players who consistently improve across several measures.
Players whose physical and football-skill results differ significantly.
Whether benchmark groups are large enough to be useful.
Whether recorded data leads to a practical coaching action.
progressions: Create trend graphs across the season.
Link testing results to individual development plans.
Compare training tests with match statistics.
Add confidence intervals or reliability ranges for repeated tests.
Create squad-level reports for coaching review.
regressions: Use a simple paper-based player record.
Track only three to five key measures.
Compare current results only with the player’s own baseline.
Remove rankings and use development categories.
Enter data after each station rather than after the full session.
successIndicators: Record complete and accurate raw results.
Identify the test version and conditions.
Separate valid, modified and invalid attempts.
Convert results into practical development actions.
Reproduce calculations when results are reviewed.
matchApplication: Testing data becomes valuable only when it improves coaching decisions. A reliable record system helps coaches identify development priorities, monitor progress, adjust training, support role decisions and provide evidence-based player feedback.

title: Integrated Foundation Testing Battery
objective: Complete a repeatable foundation testing battery that combines technical, movement and decision-making measures into one organised player-assessment session.
groundSize: Half an oval or an equivalent area divided into six testing stations.
setup:
Divide the testing area into six stations:
Kicking accuracy.
Handball accuracy and release.
Marking reliability.
Ground-ball collection.
Football movement and agility.
Decision-making small-sided game.
Assign a trained coach or recorder to every station.
Divide the squad into balanced testing groups.
Prepare a rotation schedule with defined work and transition periods.
Complete a standardised warm-up before Station One.
Place the highest-speed station early enough that players are not excessively fatigued.
Prepare modified versions for injured, younger or masters players.
Use one central data-control point to receive completed station sheets.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a 12- to 15-minute standardised warm-up.
The testing coordinator explains each station, scoring process and rotation.
Groups begin at assigned stations.
Each station operates for eight to twelve minutes, followed by a two-minute transition.
Players complete the published repetitions without receiving technical coaching during scored attempts.
Station coaches record raw scores, validity, conditions and brief observations.
After five technical and movement stations, players receive a short recovery period.
The squad completes the decision-making game in balanced teams.
Coaches independently record the required decision-making behaviours.
All station records are checked at the central data point.
Players complete a short cool-down and are told when feedback will be provided.
Results are entered into the player-testing system and reviewed before individual conclusions are made.
coachingPoints: Standardise instructions before testing starts.
Train station staff in scoring and invalid-attempt rules.
Keep rotation times consistent.
Separate assessment from technical coaching.
Provide enough recovery for valid performance.
Record test modifications clearly.
Check equipment and surface safety before every rotation.
Avoid over-interpreting one poor station.
Compare results with player profiles, roles and previous testing.
Provide feedback after data has been checked.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether station instructions are applied consistently.
Technical performance across multiple skill areas.
Differences between isolated skill results and decision-making performance.
Whether one station creates delays or excessive waiting.
Player behaviour and response after mistakes.
progressions: Introduce pressure versions of technical tests.
Add controlled fatigue before selected football skills.
Use video recording for later technical review.
Compare pre-season, mid-season and post-season batteries.
Develop separate pathway, senior and masters benchmark groups.
Add match-performance review after the testing session.
regressions: Conduct the battery across two training nights.
Reduce the number of repetitions at each station.
Use four core stations for younger players.
Replace the decision-making game with a simpler overload activity.
Provide longer recovery and shorter movement distances.
Allow injured players to complete only approved stations.
successIndicators: Understand and complete each testing protocol.
Produce valid results across the required stations.
Maintain safe movement and football technique.
Demonstrate measurable strengths and development priorities.
Complete the battery without excessive standing or confusion.
Link results to player roles and development plans.
Provide balanced feedback based on multiple measures.
matchApplication: The integrated battery creates a broad picture of how a player moves, executes skills and makes decisions. It prevents assessment from relying on one athletic result or one isolated football skill and provides a structured foundation for individual development planning, squad training priorities and later advanced testing.

title: Handball Accuracy and Release-Speed Test
objective: Measure each player’s handball accuracy and release speed from stationary, moving and non-preferred-side conditions using a standardised testing sequence.
groundSize: A 20 × 15 metre area with handball stations at 5, 8 and 12 metres.
equipment: Target boards or marked target gates
setup:
Establish target stations at 5, 8 and 12 metres.
Use a target board, net or marked receiving gate approximately 1.5 metres wide.
Mark a receiving cone three metres before the handball line for the moving test.
Prepare one preferred-side and one non-preferred-side station.
Nominate a consistent feeder, timer and recorder.
Define release time as the period from secure possession to football leaving the hand.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each player completes three practice handballs on each side.
The player performs ten stationary preferred-side handballs at the eight-metre target.
The player performs ten stationary non-preferred-side handballs at the same target.
The player receives a feed while moving through the approach cone and completes five preferred-side handballs.
The player repeats the moving test on the non-preferred side.
For advanced players, five handballs are completed at 12 metres.
The timer records release time for the moving repetitions.
Award two points for hitting the central target, one point for entering the receiving gate and zero points for missing.
Record accuracy, average release time, fastest controlled release and technical observations.
Rotate players through feeder, receiver, recorder and testing roles.
coachingPoints: Keep feed speed and placement consistent.
Time only repetitions where the player gains secure possession.
Do not reward fast release when the handball is inaccurate.
Record preferred- and non-preferred-side results separately.
Maintain identical target dimensions for all players.
Use the same definition of a successful handball throughout the squad.
Allow adequate recovery so fatigue does not distort the technical baseline.
Note whether the player steps towards the target or handballs across the body.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Contact point of the striking fist.
Whether the football travels with a stable flight.
Accuracy differences between stationary and moving attempts.
Release-speed differences between preferred and non-preferred sides.
Whether the player needs extra steps before releasing.
Whether rushed repetitions become throws or uncontrolled contacts.
progressions: Require the player to identify a coloured target before releasing.
Add handballs after a ground-ball collection.
Add a turn or change of direction before the receive.
Add a fatigue block before repeating the final set.
regressions: Test five repetitions per side rather than ten.
Delay release-time measurement until technique is reliable.
successIndicators: Hit the defined target area with legal handballs.
Demonstrate a measurable result on both sides.
Maintain body control while receiving on the move.
Produce repeatable performance across the test.
matchApplication: The test measures a player’s ability to release the football accurately in congestion, link with a running teammate and use either side of the body. These actions directly influence stoppage exits, overlap running, defensive releases and attacking chains.

title: Ground-Ball Clean Collection Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to approach, collect and control ground-level footballs cleanly from stationary, moving and angled feeds.
groundSize: A 25 × 20 metre area with three collection lanes.
setup:
Establish three lanes: straight approach, angled approach and moving-football collection.
Mark a starting cone ten metres from the football.
Place a disposal target five metres beyond the collection point.
Nominate one feeder, one timer and one recorder.
Define a clean collection as secure one-touch possession without the player stopping completely or losing control.
Ensure the surface is safe and free of holes or loose equipment.
howTheDrillWorks:
Each player completes two practice collections in each lane.
In the straight lane, the player accelerates from the starting cone and collects five stationary footballs.
In the angled lane, the player completes five collections while approaching from alternating left and right angles.
In the moving-football lane, the feeder rolls five footballs at a controlled speed across the player’s path.
After each collection, the player handballs through the target gate.
Award two points for a clean collection and accurate disposal, one point for a clean collection with an inaccurate disposal, and zero points for a fumble or missed collection.
Record the time for each five-repetition set.
Record whether errors occur before contact, at contact or during the first disposal.
Rotate players through testing, feeding, recording and football-return roles.
Calculate clean-collection percentage and combined collection-and-disposal percentage.
coachingPoints: Keep feed speed consistent.
Test collection quality before adding opponent pressure.
Record whether the player slows excessively before the football.
Distinguish a one-touch gather from possession completed after a fumble.
Require the head and shoulders to remain balanced through the collection.
Count disposal accuracy separately where required.
Use the same surface and football condition for all tested players.
Allow sufficient recovery between sets.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Speed adjustment during the final steps.
Whether the player gets the body behind the football.
Hand position close to ground level.
Clean control on the first contact.
Ability to collect from both approach angles.
progressions: Add a choice between kick and handball targets.
Begin with the player facing away from the football before reacting to a cue.
regressions: Allow younger players to complete fewer repetitions.
successIndicators: Adjust approach speed without losing momentum.
Collect the football cleanly in one action.
Maintain body position behind the football.
Complete an effective disposal after collection.
Produce similar results from both approach angles.
matchApplication: Ground-ball reliability is essential at stoppages, in defensive contests, during forward pressure and after loose-football turnovers. The test shows whether a player can secure possession cleanly while maintaining enough balance and momentum to complete the next football action.

title: Marking Reliability and Ball-Judgement Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to judge the football and complete uncontested chest, overhead and lead-up marks from repeatable deliveries.
groundSize: A 35 × 25 metre area with three marking lanes.
setup:
Create three lanes for chest marks, overhead marks and lead-up marks.
Position the feeder 15–25 metres from the marking player depending on age and ability.
Mark a two-metre receiving zone for the stationary tests.
Mark a ten-metre lead channel for the moving test.
Use one consistent feeder per station where possible.
Define a completed mark as secure control without the football touching the ground.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete two practice repetitions at each station.
At Station One, each player attempts ten chest marks from controlled kicks.
At Station Two, each player attempts ten overhead marks delivered above eye level.
At Station Three, each player completes ten lead-up marks into the marked channel.
Award one point for every clean mark.
Record whether dropped marks result from poor delivery, misjudgement, hand position or loss of control.
Record the player’s first action after any dropped mark.
Advanced groups may include five marks delivered slightly left and five slightly right of the player’s starting line.
Rotate players through marking, feeding, football return and recording roles.
Calculate an overall mark-completion percentage and separate percentages for each mark type.
coachingPoints: Standardise the quality and distance of deliveries.
Exclude clearly untestable kicks and repeat them.
Record clean control rather than whether the player touched the football.
Assess ball judgement separately from hand strength.
Do not provide corrective coaching during the scored set.
Observe whether the player moves early to the drop zone.
Record recovery behaviour after dropped marks.
Modify delivery height and distance for younger players without changing the assessment purpose.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Foot movement towards the drop zone.
Whether the player marks at the highest practical point.
Body balance at the moment of contact.
Ability to maintain control through the landing.
Immediate reaction after a dropped mark.
progressions: Add marks after a change of direction.
Add wet-football testing under safe conditions.
Add position-specific deliveries such as defensive intercepts or forward leads.
Require an immediate disposal after the mark.
regressions: Use shorter hand or kick feeds.
Test chest marking before introducing overhead marking.
Use a lighter junior football where appropriate.
Allow the player to begin moving before the delivery.
successIndicators: Move into the correct drop zone.
Complete a high percentage of testable marks.
Track the football without turning away.
Recover quickly after an unsuccessful attempt.
Produce repeatable results across marking types.
matchApplication: Reliable marking allows a team to retain possession, intercept opposition attacks, provide forward targets and control field position. The test identifies whether errors are caused by ball judgement, movement, hand position, confidence or delivery conditions.

title: Football Movement and Agility Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to accelerate, change direction, carry the football and complete a controlled disposal through a repeatable football-specific agility course.
groundSize: A 30 × 20 metre testing area.
setup:
Mark a start line and a five-metre acceleration gate.
Place change-of-direction cones at 5, 10 and 15 metres.
Create one lateral cut, one 180-degree turn and one curved running line.
Position a football at the first change-of-direction cone.
Place a target gate 15 metres beyond the final turn.
Define the finish as the moment the football passes through the target gate or crosses the target line.
Provide a separate deceleration area beyond the finish.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised movement and football warm-up.
Each player walks through the course once.
On the start signal, the player accelerates to the first cone.
The player collects the football and completes the marked change-of-direction pattern.
The player performs one legal bounce in the designated section.
At the final cone, the player steadies and kicks through the target gate.
Time begins on the start signal and stops when the kick crosses the target line.
Add a time penalty for missing the target gate or failing to complete the required bounce.
Each player completes three trials with full recovery.
Record the best valid time, average time, disposal accuracy and movement observations.
coachingPoints: Use the same course dimensions for every player.
Complete a thorough warm-up before maximal trials.
Separate raw course time from time penalties.
Do not allow unsafe cutting technique to be rewarded.
Record both best time and average consistency.
Ensure the football is positioned identically for every trial.
Provide full recovery between maximal attempts.
Modify turn angles and total distance for younger players and masters footballers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Body height before each change of direction.
Foot placement and balance through cuts.
Ability to collect the football without losing speed.
Whether the player regains control before kicking.
progressions: Add a reactive colour or direction cue.
Add a handball option at the finish.
Add a second football skill during the course.
Test after a controlled conditioning block.
Compare ball-carrying time with a no-football agility time.
regressions: Use submaximal trials for returning or older players.
Allow a handball finish instead of a kick.
successIndicators: Maintain balance through changes of direction.
Secure the football cleanly while moving.
Execute an accurate disposal after high-speed movement.
Produce consistent times across valid trials.
matchApplication: Australian football requires players to accelerate into space, change direction around pressure, carry the football and execute after movement. This test combines physical movement with football control so that athletic speed is assessed alongside functional match skill.

title: Coach Rating Calibration and Reliability Exercise
objective: Improve the consistency of coach ratings by requiring multiple coaches to assess the same football behaviours independently and then calibrate their use of the approved observation scale.
players: Minimum: 8 players and 2 coaches Ideal: 12–18 players and 3–5 coaches Maximum: Full Squad
groundSize: A 40 × 30 metre small-sided game area plus a separate coach discussion area.
physicalLoad: 3 – Moderate for players; 1 – Very Low for coaches
setup:
Select three to five clearly defined behaviours to assess.
Examples include scanning before possession, defensive positioning, disposal choice, support movement and turnover reaction.
Define the evidence required for ratings one to five.
Assign the same players to each observer.
Position coaches separately so they cannot influence one another during assessment.
Prepare a post-assessment comparison sheet.
howTheDrillWorks:
Coaches review the written definitions for each assessed behaviour.
Players complete a four-minute small-sided game.
Every coach independently rates the same assigned players.
Coaches record at least one observable example supporting each rating.
A second four-minute period is played with players rotating roles.
Coaches again rate the same behaviours without discussing scores.
Ratings are compared after both periods.
Where scores differ by more than one point, each coach presents the evidence used.
The coaching group agrees on clearer rating anchors or examples.
A final period is played and rated to determine whether agreement improves.
Updated definitions are recorded for future assessment sessions.
coachingPoints: Require evidence for every high or low rating.
Discuss behaviour rather than defending personal judgement.
Identify whether disagreement comes from observation, definition or weighting.
Avoid allowing the senior coach’s score to automatically become correct.
Use the same scale language across all coaching groups.
Separate role-specific expectations from general football behaviours.
Record uncertainty rather than inventing false precision.
Recalibrate regularly across a long season.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The level of agreement between coaches.
Whether coaches use the full rating scale.
Which behaviours produce the largest scoring differences.
Whether ratings are influenced by reputation or position.
Whether coaches can provide specific examples.
Whether rating definitions require clearer language.
Whether one observer consistently scores higher or lower than others.
progressions: Use recorded match vision for calibration.
Compare line-coach ratings with whole-team coach ratings.
Calculate average rating differences between observers.
Repeat the exercise with tactical and leadership behaviours.
Introduce blind player identification during video review where practical.
regressions: Observe a short, controlled drill rather than a game.
Provide example clips before live assessment.
Pair an experienced assessor with a developing coach after independent scoring.
successIndicators: Produce ratings within one point of other trained observers.
Reduce reputation, recency and positional bias.
matchApplication: Reliable coaching assessment is essential for selection, player development, role allocation and feedback. When coaches apply different standards, players receive inconsistent messages. Calibration improves confidence that ratings reflect football behaviour rather than observer preference.

title: Short-Kick Decision and Execution Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to identify the correct short-kicking option and execute an accurate, markable disposal within a controlled time limit.
groundSize: A 30 × 25 metre area containing three short-kick targets.
setup:
Place the tested player inside a five-metre starting square.
Position three target players or target gates at distances of 15–25 metres.
Give each target a different colour.
Position one target in the corridor and two on wider angles.
Nominate a coach or feeder to provide the football.
Prepare a random cue sequence identifying the correct target.
Define the disposal-time limit from secure possession to the football leaving the boot.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins facing away from the targets.
The feeder calls the player’s name and delivers the football.
As the player turns, the coach displays or calls a colour.
The player scans, identifies the matching target and completes the kick.
The kick must be released within the prescribed time limit.
Each player completes five preferred-foot and five non-preferred-foot attempts.
Award two points for an accurate kick to the correct target, one point for selecting the correct target but delivering an unmarkable kick, and zero points for choosing the wrong target.
Record decision accuracy, kicking accuracy and release time separately.
Players rotate through feeder, target, football-return and testing roles.
Repeat any feed that prevents the player from gaining reasonable possession.
coachingPoints: Keep target locations consistent across all tested players.
Randomise the colour sequence without creating a predictable pattern.
Record target selection separately from kicking execution.
Do not coach the player during scored attempts.
Apply the same release-time limit to comparable players.
Note whether players scan all options or react only to the first visible target.
Test both sides without allowing the player to reposition excessively.
Repeat the assessment under the same conditions during future testing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Head and eye movement immediately after turning.
Whether the player establishes balance before kicking.
Accuracy and trajectory of the kick.
Differences between preferred and non-preferred sides.
Whether time pressure causes rushed technique.
progressions: Add one defender who can close one target.
Require the player to kick after lateral movement.
Add field-position cues that alter which target is preferred.
regressions: Allow the player to begin facing the targets.
successIndicators: Avoid rushing their ball drop under time pressure.
matchApplication: Short kicking underpins possession retention, defensive exits, switches and controlled forward movement. The test separates a player’s ability to recognise the correct option from their ability to execute the required kick.

title: Long-Kick Distance and Accuracy Test
objective: Measure each player’s controllable kicking distance and directional accuracy without rewarding maximum distance at the expense of useful football execution.
groundSize: A 70 × 35 metre kicking corridor.
equipment: Measuring tape or marked distance lines
setup:
Mark a central kicking line.
Mark distance lines at five-metre intervals from 25 to 60 metres.
Create a five-metre-wide landing corridor.
Position a recorder beside the distance markings.
Establish a safe retrieval lane outside the target corridor.
Record wind direction and surface conditions.
Modify maximum distances for age and capability.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a progressive kicking warm-up.
Each player performs three practice kicks.
The player completes five preferred-foot long kicks.
The player then completes three non-preferred-foot long kicks.
Measure the distance from the kicking line to the first ground contact.
Record whether the football lands inside the target corridor.
A kick counts as a controlled maximum only when it reaches the distance and lands inside the corridor.
Record the longest accurate kick, average accurate distance and overall corridor accuracy.
Exclude kicks affected by interruptions or unsafe retrieval movement.
Rotate players through kicking, recording and football-return roles.
coachingPoints: Measure useful football distance rather than total roll.
Record wind and surface conditions.
Require a stable starting position for each attempt.
Do not allow players to step beyond the kicking line.
Separate longest kick from longest accurate kick.
Observe whether greater effort changes the ball drop or contact quality.
Allow full recovery between maximal kicks.
Avoid excessive maximal attempts.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Difference between preferred and non-preferred sides.
progressions: Test long kicking after a five-metre run.
Add a moving target at the end of the corridor.
Compare long-kick performance from both field sides.
successIndicators: Keep the football within a useful trajectory.
Avoid major technical breakdown at maximal effort.
Produce results that can be repeated under comparable conditions.
matchApplication: Long kicking is required for defensive exits, switches, forward entries, kick-ins and scoring opportunities. This assessment identifies the maximum distance at which a player can still deliver a controlled and tactically useful football.

title: Goal-Kicking Routine and Conversion Test
objective: Assess each player’s goal-kicking conversion, routine consistency and miss pattern across controlled distances and angles.
groundSize: One forward-50 area with six marked set-shot positions.
setup:
Mark six shot locations:
Two directly in front.
Two from the left side.
Two from the right side.
Use distances appropriate to the age and competition level.
Mark a standard starting point for each shot.
Position recorders behind the kicker and near the goals.
Define the permitted preparation time.
Record wind conditions before testing.
Establish a safe football-return system outside the kicking line.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a progressive goal-kicking warm-up.
Each player completes two non-scored practice shots.
The player attempts two scored shots from each marked position.
Players use their normal set-shot routine.
The recorder notes routine duration, starting line, kick type, result and miss direction.
Award one point for a goal and zero for a behind or out on the full.
Record shots falling short separately from directional misses.
Calculate total conversion and conversion by distance and side.
Record whether routine steps remain consistent after misses.
Players rotate through kicking, recording and football-return roles.
coachingPoints: Use the same shot locations for every comparable player.
Avoid technical coaching during the scored sequence.
Record the type and direction of each miss.
Note routine consistency rather than imposing one routine.
Separate distance limitations from accuracy errors.
Allow sufficient recovery between longer shots.
Test in comparable wind conditions where possible.
Use age-appropriate distances.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Change in routine after a miss.
Conversion differences by angle and distance.
progressions: Add a shot after a short lead and mark.
Include a snap set shot where competition rules and player role make it relevant.
Test after a controlled running effort.
Compare practice conversion with match conversion.
regressions: Widen the acceptable target for younger players.
Complete the test over two sessions.
successIndicators: Convert at an age- and role-appropriate rate.
Reset their process after an unsuccessful shot.
Maintain conversion from both sides of the ground.
matchApplication: Set-shot conversion directly affects scoreboard outcomes. The test helps coaches distinguish technical errors, range limitations, angle-specific difficulties and routine breakdowns under repeated scoring demands.

title: Technical Assessment Review Circuit
objective: Complete a structured review circuit that confirms technical testing results across the first twenty Testing and Assessment records and identifies individual priorities for the next development phase.
groundSize: Half an oval divided into six to eight assessment stations.
setup:
Select six to eight stations appropriate to the squad:
Short-kick decision and execution.
Long-kick distance and accuracy.
Goal-kicking conversion.
Contested marking.
Spoiling direction.
Tackling technique.
Ruck accuracy or stoppage-role execution.
Defensive transition.
Prepare standard instructions and scoring sheets at each station.
Assign trained staff to all contact and tactical stations.
Divide the squad into balanced groups.
Establish rotation and recovery periods.
Prepare non-contact alternatives for modified players.
Confirm that previous baseline results are available for comparison.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised 15-minute warm-up.
The testing coordinator explains all station rules and scoring procedures.
Groups begin at assigned stations.
Each station operates for eight to twelve minutes.
Players complete the published attempts without technical coaching during scored repetitions.
Station coaches record raw results and observable behaviours.
Groups rotate on the central signal.
Contact stations are completed only under direct qualified supervision.
Players receive a recovery break before transition or stoppage testing.
All records are returned to the central data point.
Results are checked against previous baselines.
Each player is assigned one confirmed strength, one priority technical skill and one next-step training action.
coachingPoints: Select stations relevant to the age and role of the squad.
Use identical scoring standards across groups.
Compare results with previous tests rather than relying only on squad rankings.
Do not combine unrelated measures into one overall player score.
Record modified tests clearly.
Prioritise safety at contact and maximal-effort stations.
Provide enough recovery for reliable performance.
Link every identified weakness to a practical training response.
Confirm unusual results before reporting them.
Provide balanced feedback.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Differences between isolated technique and pressure performance.
Technical breakdown under speed or contact.
Whether previous development priorities have improved.
Whether testing results lead to clear coaching actions.
progressions: Compare fresh and fatigued technical performance.
Add coach and player self-rating comparisons.
Conduct the circuit at multiple points across the season.
regressions: Split the circuit across two sessions.
Replace tactical games with controlled decision drills.
Compare players only with their own prior baseline.
successIndicators: Complete valid assessments across relevant skill areas.
Demonstrate measurable strengths and development needs.
Convert findings into individual and squad training plans.
matchApplication: The review circuit brings together technical, contest and tactical assessments so coaches can understand how each player performs across the major demands of Australian football. It provides a controlled checkpoint before moving into more advanced testing, pressure assessment and role-specific evaluation.

title: Contested Marking Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to establish position, judge the football and complete or neutralise a controlled one-on-one marking contest.
groundSize: A 35 × 25 metre area with two marking lanes.
setup:
Create two marking lanes approximately 25 metres long and eight metres wide.
Place one attacker and one defender inside each lane.
Position a consistent kicker at the delivery cone.
Mark a legal contest zone.
Establish clear body-contact and safety rules.
Pair players by size, age and experience.
Prepare scoring criteria for win, neutral result and loss.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker and defender begin side by side or in a nominated front-and-back position.
On the coach’s signal, both players move into the contest zone.
The kicker delivers a high, testable football.
The attacker attempts to mark while the defender contests legally.
Award two points for a clean contested mark, one point for bringing the football to ground and retaining or neutralising the contest, and zero points for losing the contest clearly.
Each player completes five repetitions as attacker and five as defender.
Alternate starting positions and delivery sides.
Record body position, flight judgement, contact legality and contest outcome.
Stop any repetition where the delivery creates unsafe contact.
Rotate pairs and feeders after the set.
coachingPoints: Pair players appropriately.
Use controlled, legal body contact.
Deliver footballs that create genuine but safe contests.
Record positioning and judgement, not only the final mark.
Separate attacking and defensive results.
Stop players from holding, pushing in the back or making front-on contact.
Allow recovery between repetitions.
Record how the player responds when the football reaches ground level.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to neutralise a lost aerial position.
progressions: Add a second defender or supporting crumber.
Add a short lead before the contest.
Add immediate disposal after a completed mark.
regressions: Replace aerial contests with protected marking.
Use a pad rather than a live opponent.
successIndicators: Establish or challenge for effective body position.
Complete or neutralise a high proportion of contests.
React immediately when the football reaches ground level.
matchApplication: Contested marking affects forward targets, defensive intercepts, wing contests and stoppage exits. This assessment identifies whether a player’s contest performance is limited by positioning, judgement, timing, hand strength or recovery.

title: Spoiling Direction and Recovery Test
objective: Assess each defender’s ability to position correctly, spoil legally and direct the football towards a safer defensive area before recovering into the next action.
groundSize: A 35 × 30 metre defensive contest area.
setup:
Mark a central aerial-contest zone.
Place a safe defensive scoring zone towards the boundary.
Place a neutral zone in front of the contest.
Mark a dangerous opposition scoring zone towards the corridor.
Position one attacker and one defender in the contest area.
Use a consistent kicker from 20–30 metres.
Establish legal-contact and front-on-contact restrictions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defender begins behind or beside the attacker.
On the signal, the kicker delivers a high football into the contest zone.
The attacker attempts to mark.
The defender attempts to spoil legally.
Award three points for a legal spoil into the safe zone, two points for a legal spoil into the neutral zone, one point for bringing the football straight to ground, and zero points for a dangerous-zone spoil or lost contest.
The contest continues for three seconds after the football reaches ground level.
Record the defender’s recovery action.
Each defender completes six to ten repetitions from varied starting positions.
Repeat untestable or unsafe deliveries.
Rotate attackers, defenders, kickers and recorders.
coachingPoints: Assess direction as well as contact with the football.
Require legal fist contact.
Observe the defender’s starting position relative to the attacker.
Record whether the defender keeps vision of the football.
Do not reward uncontrolled spoils into dangerous space.
Continue the repetition briefly after the aerial contest.
Match opponents appropriately.
Apply strict safety controls.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to maintain contact without holding.
Recovery to the football or opponent.
progressions: Add two attackers against one defender.
Add a defensive teammate calling the preferred spoil direction.
Add immediate defensive exit after recovery.
regressions: Begin the defender in front position.
successIndicators: Make effective contact with the football.
Recover immediately into the next defensive action.
matchApplication: Effective spoiling is not simply preventing a mark. Defenders must reduce opposition scoring chances by directing the football towards the boundary, teammates or low-risk space and then remaining involved in the contest.

title: Tackling Technique and Pressure Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to track, make legal contact, control the ball carrier and recover safely through a series of standardised tackling situations.
groundSize: A 20 × 15 metre controlled contact area.
setup:
Create three tackling lanes:
Stationary contact.
Tracking from an angle.
Controlled live tackle.
Mark a five-metre entry channel and safe finish zone.
Pair players according to size and experience.
Establish tackle-height, release and safety rules.
Position a trained coach at every live-contact station.
Prepare an assessment scale covering tracking, contact, control, legality and recovery.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a contact-preparation warm-up.
At Station One, the player demonstrates three controlled tackles on a bag.
At Station Two, the player tracks a ball carrier moving at controlled speed and applies three wrap tackles without taking the player to ground.
At Station Three, the ball carrier attempts to cross a five-metre line while the tackler completes a legal controlled tackle.
Each player completes five live repetitions from alternating approach angles.
Award one point each for controlled approach, legal contact height, secure wrap, stopping or redirecting the carrier, and safe release.
Record any unsafe or illegal action immediately.
Assess the tackler’s balance and ability to recover after contact.
Rotate players through tackler, carrier and observer roles.
Stop the assessment if fatigue reduces safety or control.
coachingPoints: Prioritise safety and legality over force.
Assess the approach before contact.
Require the tackler to shorten steps and maintain balance.
Match players appropriately.
Do not reward high contact, sling actions or dangerous driving.
Record control of the ball carrier rather than impact sound.
Assess release and recovery after the whistle.
Use tackle bags before live assessment.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to stop or redirect the carrier.
Balance and repeat effort after contact.
progressions: Add a disposal decision for the ball carrier.
Introduce a second effort after the first tackle.
Add a teammate applying front-on pressure.
Use match-like contact for suitably prepared senior players.
successIndicators: Recover into the next defensive action.
matchApplication: Tackling effectiveness depends on tracking, legal contact, control and recovery rather than force alone. This assessment identifies technical and safety weaknesses that affect pressure, stoppage defence and turnover creation.

title: Defensive Transition Response Test
objective: Assess how quickly and effectively players recognise a turnover, organise defensive roles and protect dangerous space during an immediate transition.
groundSize: A 60 × 45 metre area with attacking and defensive scoring gates.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Mark a central possession zone and two scoring gates at each end.
Establish a normal attacking direction.
Prepare a series of planned turnover signals.
Assign observers to specific players.
Define assessment categories: recognition, first three steps, role choice, communication, corridor protection and pressure.
Use controlled contact rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins with uncontested possession in the central zone.
After three to five disposals, the coach signals or creates a turnover.
The previous attacking team must immediately transition into defence.
The new attacking team attempts to score through either gate within ten seconds.
Observers rate assigned players from the moment possession changes.
Play continues until a score, interception or ten-second limit.
Reset and repeat with a different turnover location.
Complete eight to twelve transitions.
Rotate player positions between blocks.
Compare individual response patterns across central, wide and defensive turnovers.
coachingPoints: Observe the instant possession changes.
Record the first three steps.
Assess whether players protect dangerous space before chasing the football.
Note communication and opponent identification.
Separate effort from effective defensive action.
Use several turnover locations.
Avoid giving transition instructions during scored repetitions.
Provide sufficient recovery between high-speed blocks.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player protects space or ball-watches.
Recovery after the first defensive action.
progressions: Remove the coach signal and use genuine live turnovers.
regressions: Pause after the turnover to identify roles.
successIndicators: Slow or stop the opposition attack.
Continue working after the first pressure action.
matchApplication: Turnovers create some of the most dangerous moments in Australian football. This assessment identifies players who react with effective defensive intent rather than remaining in attacking positions, ball-watching or chasing without structure.

title: Ruck Hit-Zone Accuracy Test
objective: Measure a ruck player’s ability to direct controlled hit-outs into nominated teammate zones from standardised ball-ups and boundary-style feeds.
groundSize: A 20 × 20 metre stoppage-testing area.
setup:
Mark four receiving zones around a central ruck point:
Front.
Left.
Right.
Rear.
Make each zone approximately three metres wide.
Position a consistent thrower or ball-up coach.
Nominate a receiver in each zone.
Prepare a random sequence of zone calls.
Begin with uncontested ruck work before adding an opponent.
Define a successful hit-out as a controlled touch reaching the nominated receiving zone.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ruck completes a jumping and contact warm-up.
The coach calls a coloured or numbered hit zone before the ball-up.
The ruck attempts to direct the football into that zone.
Each player completes five attempts to each zone.
Award two points when the nominated receiver can gather without moving more than one step, one point when the football enters the zone but requires adjustment, and zero points when it misses.
Record clean-contact rate and zone accuracy.
Complete a second set using boundary-style feeds.
Advanced players repeat selected attempts against controlled opposition.
Record the ruck’s landing balance and first follow-up movement.
Rotate rucks, receivers, feeders and recorders.
coachingPoints: Use consistent feeds.
Assess direction separately from winning height.
Record whether the ruck uses palm, fist or fingertip contact.
Observe setup and jump timing.
Require safe landing mechanics.
Avoid excessive jumping volume.
Retest using the same zone dimensions.
Record uncontested and opposed results separately.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Height and speed of the hit.
progressions: Delay the zone cue until the ball is in flight.
Add a clearance action after the hit-out.
regressions: Use a ruck pad instead of an opponent.
successIndicators: Direct the football towards the nominated zone.
Follow the hit-out into the next phase.
matchApplication: A hit-out is most valuable when it creates advantage for a midfielder. This test measures whether the ruck can control direction and weight rather than simply reaching the football first.

title: Stoppage Role Execution Assessment
objective: Assess how consistently players perform their assigned stoppage roles before, during and immediately after a controlled stoppage contest.
groundSize: A 30 × 30 metre stoppage area with two exit gates.
setup:
Create two balanced stoppage groups.
Assign each player a defined role such as first possession, defensive sweeper, outside release, opposition body check or exit support.
Mark two clearance gates.
Establish legal contact rules.
Prepare role-specific observation criteria.
Assign observers to individual players or roles.
Begin from repeated ball-ups or boundary-style feeds.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players receive their role instructions before the assessment begins.
The coach restarts play from the central stoppage point.
Teams attempt to win possession and move the football through either exit gate.
Play continues for six to eight seconds after the clearance or turnover.
Observers rate starting position, role execution, communication, decision quality and post-clearance reaction.
Complete six stoppages before rotating roles.
Players perform at least two different roles.
Coaches do not provide tactical corrections during the scored block.
Ratings are supported by specific observed examples.
Finish with one open stoppage block where players select roles independently.
coachingPoints: Define each role clearly before testing.
Assess whether the player performs the role, not whether their team wins every clearance.
Observe behaviour before the ball reaches the ruck contest.
Record communication and teammate connection.
Continue observation after possession leaves the stoppage.
Separate physical contest outcomes from tactical understanding.
Use repeated stoppages to reduce the influence of one result.
Apply role-appropriate standards.
progressions: Change the ruck plan without warning.
Include full match-like contact for suitable players.
Use video review after live rating.
regressions: Test one role at a time.
successIndicators: Adapt when performing a different role.
matchApplication: Stoppage performance depends on coordinated roles rather than isolated possession counts. This assessment identifies players who understand structure, create space, protect teammates, defend opponents and connect the first possession to the next phase.

title: Ten-Metre Acceleration and Football Collection Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to accelerate over ten metres, collect a football cleanly at speed and complete an effective disposal without losing movement efficiency.
groundSize: A 25 × 15 metre testing lane.
setup:
Mark a starting line and a ten-metre timing line.
Position a stationary football at the eight-metre point.
Place a two-metre-wide handball target five metres beyond the timing line.
Establish a safe deceleration zone beyond the target.
Use the same football position and target dimensions for every player.
Prepare separate recording columns for sprint time, collection quality and disposal accuracy.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised acceleration and ground-ball warm-up.
Each player receives one walk-through and two practice attempts.
The player begins in a balanced two-point stance behind the starting line.
On the signal, the player accelerates towards the football.
The player collects the football without stopping and continues through the ten-metre timing line.
After crossing the timing line, the player handballs through the target gate.
Timing begins on the start signal and ends when the player’s torso crosses the ten-metre line.
Record the sprint time, whether the collection was clean and whether the handball was accurate.
Each player completes three valid attempts with two minutes of recovery.
Record the fastest valid attempt and the average of all valid attempts.
coachingPoints: Use an identical starting command for every player.
Require the player to begin completely behind the line.
Position the football consistently.
Separate acceleration time from skill-quality scoring.
Do not count a fumbled collection as a clean attempt.
Allow enough recovery for maximal acceleration.
Observe whether players lower their body effectively without overstriding.
Stop the test if the surface becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the football is secured in one action.
Ability to continue accelerating after collection.
Handball accuracy after the timed effort.
progressions: Begin from a prone or lateral position.
Compare the result with a ten-metre sprint without a football collection.
regressions: Begin the player closer to the football.
successIndicators: React promptly to the start signal.
Maintain speed through the timing line.
Complete an accurate disposal after acceleration.
matchApplication: Players frequently accelerate towards loose footballs before collecting and releasing under pressure. This test identifies whether a player can combine first-step speed with clean possession rather than producing speed only in a football-free sprint.

title: Twenty-Metre Sprint and Ball-Carry Test
primarySkill: Sprint speed while carrying the football
objective: Measure each player’s ability to accelerate and maintain speed over twenty metres while securely carrying and legally bouncing the football.
groundSize: A straight 35 × 8 metre running corridor.
setup:
Mark a start line, ten-metre split and twenty-metre finish line.
Mark a bounce zone between eight and twelve metres.
Provide a fifteen-metre deceleration area beyond the finish.
Use timing gates where available.
Prepare separate result columns for total time, ten-metre split, bounce validity and ball security.
Ensure the running surface is level and dry.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a sprint and bouncing warm-up.
Each player performs one walk-through and two progressive runs.
The player begins behind the starting line holding the football.
On the signal, the player accelerates through the lane.
The player must complete one legal bounce inside the marked bounce zone.
The player continues at maximum controlled speed through the twenty-metre finish.
Record the ten-metre split and total twenty-metre time.
Mark the trial invalid if the bounce occurs outside the zone or possession is lost.
Each player completes three valid attempts with full recovery.
Record the fastest valid time and the variation between attempts.
coachingPoints: Require players to run through the finish rather than slowing early.
Use the same football size and condition for all comparable players.
Do not allow the football to be thrown forward and regathered.
Separate speed from bounce validity.
Provide two to three minutes of recovery.
Record whether the football changes the player’s normal running action.
Use a generous deceleration area.
Modify intensity for returning and masters players.
progressions: Require the football to be carried in the non-preferred hand.
Add a disposal after the finish.
Compare ball-carry and no-football sprint times.
regressions: Reduce the distance to fifteen metres.
Allow a shorter approach for younger players.
successIndicators: Complete a legal bounce without major speed loss.
matchApplication: Players often carry the football at high speed while breaking lines, transitioning from defence or attacking open space. The test identifies whether ball carrying and bouncing significantly reduce a player’s running speed or control.

title: Repeat-Sprint Football Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to repeat short, high-intensity football efforts while maintaining movement speed, possession quality and disposal accuracy.
groundSize: A 35 × 15 metre testing corridor.
setup:
Mark a fifteen-metre outward lane and return lane.
Place a football at the far cone.
Position a handball target near the starting line.
Prepare timing for each individual repetition.
Establish a fixed recovery period of twenty seconds.
Ensure players have completed a thorough warm-up.
Prepare modified protocols for youth, masters and returning players.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins behind the starting line.
On the signal, the player sprints fifteen metres to the football.
The player collects cleanly, turns and carries the football back.
Before crossing the finish line, the player handballs through the target.
Timing begins on the start signal and ends when the player crosses the finish line.
The player receives twenty seconds of recovery.
The sequence is repeated six times.
Record every repetition time, clean-collection result and handball accuracy.
Calculate fastest time, average time and percentage performance decline.
Stop the test if technique, safety or physical condition deteriorates excessively.
coachingPoints: Use the same recovery period for every player.
Record each repetition rather than only the final time.
Separate movement decline from skill decline.
Require a legal turn around the far cone.
Do not accept unsafe diving collections.
Provide medical and conditioning oversight where appropriate.
Modify effort numbers for younger or masters players.
Avoid conducting the test after a heavy training session.
regressions: Conduct at controlled rather than maximal intensity.
matchApplication: Australian football requires repeated accelerations to contests, support positions and defensive roles. This test identifies whether a player can reproduce high-intensity efforts while still completing football actions effectively.

title: Integrated Football Movement Profile
objective: Create an individual football-movement profile by combining acceleration, speed, agility, repeat-effort, aerial and disposal assessments into a structured review battery.
groundSize: Half an oval divided into five movement-testing stations.
setup:
Establish five stations:
Ten-metre acceleration and football collection.
Twenty-metre sprint and ball carrying.
Reactive change of direction and deceleration.
Vertical jump and aerial reach.
Movement-to-disposal efficiency.
Use the repeat-sprint or intermittent-endurance test as a separate final station where appropriate.
Assign trained staff to every station.
Prepare a rotation schedule.
Use standardised warm-up and recovery periods.
Prepare age-, role- and injury-appropriate modifications.
Establish a central data-control point.
Review previous movement results before the session.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised fifteen-minute warm-up.
The coordinator explains the station order and validity rules.
Groups begin at assigned stations.
Each station operates for ten to fifteen minutes.
Players complete the standardised number of valid attempts.
Station coaches record raw times, skill outcomes and movement observations.
Players receive adequate recovery before maximal attempts.
Groups rotate on the central signal.
The repeat-sprint or endurance station is completed last where included.
All records are returned to the central data point.
Results are checked for errors, modifications and invalid attempts.
Coaches create an individual profile identifying movement strengths, football limitations and priority development areas.
coachingPoints: Avoid reducing the profile to one overall athletic score.
Interpret speed alongside football skill.
Compare each player with their own prior result.
Consider positional role and match demands.
Record modified tests separately.
Use sufficient recovery between maximal stations.
Stop testing where safe movement deteriorates.
Separate physical limitation from technical limitation.
Review unusual results before reporting them.
Link findings to training actions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Speed loss while carrying the football.
Differences between isolated physical and football-specific performance.
Whether results match observed match behaviour.
progressions: Add contact and contest movement assessments.
Conduct testing at multiple seasonal checkpoints.
regressions: Complete the profile across two sessions.
Use submaximal movement for returning players.
Compare players only with their own baseline.
Remove reactive and contact components for younger groups.
successIndicators: Receive development priorities relevant to their role.
Interpret physical and football performance together.
Convert testing information into practical training plans.
matchApplication: The integrated profile shows how effectively a player accelerates, carries, changes direction, stops, jumps, repeats efforts and disposes. It provides a more useful football picture than isolated running tests and establishes the foundation for advanced pressure and role-specific assessment.

title: Reactive Change-of-Direction Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to respond to an unpredictable visual cue, change direction efficiently and accelerate into the correct football action.
groundSize: A 20 × 20 metre testing area.
equipment: Visual cue cards or electronic light system
setup:
Place a central starting cone.
Position three coloured gates five metres forward-left, forward-centre and forward-right.
Place a football at the central cone or begin with the player holding it.
Position a coach behind the finish gates with colour cards.
Establish a timing line at each gate.
Randomise the cue sequence before testing.
Provide sufficient space beyond every gate for safe deceleration.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins in an athletic position at the central cone.
The coach presents a colour cue after a variable delay.
The player identifies the matching gate and accelerates towards it.
The player carries the football through the selected gate.
Timing begins when the cue appears and ends when the player crosses the correct gate.
Record reaction time where technology permits and total movement time in all cases.
A wrong-gate movement is recorded as a decision error.
Each player completes six trials with an even distribution of directions.
Provide at least sixty seconds of recovery between trials.
Record average valid time, fastest time, decision errors and movement observations.
coachingPoints: Keep the cue unpredictable.
Use an equal number of left, right and centre trials.
Do not allow players to anticipate from the coach’s body movement.
Record decision errors separately from movement speed.
Require controlled foot placement.
Avoid rewarding unsafe cutting.
Maintain the same starting position.
Use sufficient recovery.
progressions: Add a handball target beyond each gate.
Delay the cue until the player is already moving.
regressions: Provide a verbal and visual cue.
Allow the player to begin upright.
successIndicators: Wait for and correctly interpret the cue.
Accelerate strongly out of the turn.
matchApplication: Australian football movement is rarely pre-planned. Players must react to opponents, teammates, loose footballs and changing space. This test measures decision-linked agility rather than rehearsed cone-running speed alone.

title: Deceleration and Re-Acceleration Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to reduce speed safely, control body position and accelerate into a second football action without unnecessary delay.
groundSize: A 30 × 12 metre lane.
setup:
Mark a starting line.
Place an acceleration cone ten metres away.
Mark a three-metre deceleration zone.
Position a second gate five metres to the left or right.
Place a handball target beyond the second gate.
Alternate test direction across attempts.
Ensure all stopping and turning zones are free of surface hazards.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins holding the football behind the starting line.
On the signal, the player accelerates for ten metres.
The player must reduce speed inside the marked deceleration zone.
At the end of the zone, the coach calls left or right.
The player changes direction and re-accelerates through the second gate.
The player then handballs through the target.
Record total time, whether the player stopped within the zone and disposal accuracy.
Each player completes three left and three right trials.
Invalid trials include leaving the deceleration zone uncontrolled or moving before the direction cue.
Record average valid time and technical observations.
coachingPoints: Assess control as well as speed.
Use the same approach distance.
Require players to remain on their feet and balanced.
Record whether braking occurs before or inside the designated zone.
Alternate turning sides.
Do not reward a fast attempt that leaves the player unable to dispose effectively.
Use sufficient recovery.
Modify speed for returning or older players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Number and length of braking steps.
progressions: Add a kick instead of a handball.
Add a defender beyond the turn.
Add a second change of direction.
successIndicators: Enter the deceleration zone at speed.
Reduce momentum within the required area.
matchApplication: Players must repeatedly slow, stop and accelerate when creating separation, defending leads, responding to turnovers or preparing to dispose. Poor deceleration reduces football effectiveness and may increase injury risk.

title: Lateral Defensive Movement Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to maintain balanced defensive position, move laterally and contain an opponent without crossing the feet or losing control of dangerous space.
groundSize: A 15 × 12 metre defensive channel.
setup:
Mark a ten-metre-wide channel.
Place one scoring gate on each side.
Position an attacker with the football at one end.
Position a defender three metres away.
Establish a five-second contest limit.
Restrict contact to incidental body contact and legal corralling pressure.
Prepare an observation scale for balance, positioning, footwork, containment and recovery.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins facing the defender.
On the signal, the attacker attempts to cross either scoring gate.
The defender moves laterally to contain the attacker.
The defender may close space but may not tackle.
The repetition ends when the attacker crosses a gate, leaves the channel or the five-second limit expires.
Award the defender two points for containment, one point for forcing the attacker outside the channel and zero points when the attacker crosses under control.
Each defender completes six repetitions against varied attackers.
Record movement quality as well as outcome.
Rotate attacker and defender roles.
Provide full recovery between short maximal contests.
coachingPoints: Observe whether the defender protects the most dangerous path.
Do not reward frantic movement that gives up balance.
Require the defender to remain square for as long as practical.
Record foot crossing and over-commitment.
Use attackers of varied styles.
Maintain controlled contact rules.
Separate containment outcome from technical quality.
Stop if the surface becomes slippery.
progressions: Add a recovery sprint after containment.
regressions: Use shadow movement without a football.
Remove scoring and assess technique only.
successIndicators: Apply controlled pressure without unnecessary contact.
matchApplication: Defenders must track opponents, protect the corridor, delay ball carriers and avoid over-committing. This test assesses functional defensive movement rather than general agility alone.

title: Intermittent Running and Skill-Endurance Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to complete repeated intermittent running efforts while maintaining accurate football disposal as fatigue progressively increases.
groundSize: A 40 × 25 metre rectangular testing area.
setup:
Mark two running lines twenty metres apart.
Place a handball target at one end and a kicking target at the other.
Use a progressive audio interval schedule.
Position a football supply at both ends.
Assign one observer to each small group.
Define disposal requirements for each running level.
Prepare clear withdrawal and safety procedures.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin behind one running line.
On the audio signal, players run twenty metres to the opposite line.
At nominated intervals, the player must receive a football and complete the required disposal before the next signal.
Odd-numbered skill intervals require a handball through the target.
Even-numbered skill intervals require a short kick through the target gate.
Running speed gradually increases according to the audio schedule.
Record the final completed level, total running volume and disposal results by level.
A player receives one warning for missing the line.
The test ends after the second missed line or when the player voluntarily withdraws.
Skill accuracy is calculated for early, middle and late test stages.
coachingPoints: Use the same audio protocol for all comparable tests.
Require players to reach the line rather than turning early.
Record skill quality separately from running completion.
Standardise football feeds.
Monitor players for excessive distress.
Do not pressure an unwell or injured player to continue.
Use age-appropriate protocols.
Record environmental conditions.
successIndicators: Execute skills accurately during early stages.
Limit skill decline as fatigue rises.
Withdraw safely when unable to continue.
matchApplication: Players must execute skills during repeated periods of running, recovery and renewed effort. This assessment shows whether endurance supports football execution or whether skill quality declines sharply as physical demand increases.

title: Vertical Jump and Aerial Reach Assessment
objective: Measure each player’s standing and running aerial reach while assessing safe take-off, flight control and landing technique.
groundSize: A 20 × 15 metre testing area.
equipment: Vertical jump measuring device or marked wall
setup:
Establish a standing-reach measurement station.
Mark a safe standing vertical-jump area.
Create a five-metre running approach.
Position a suspended football or reach target where available.
Ensure the landing surface is level and clear.
Record preferred take-off leg.
Prepare separate records for standing reach, standing jump reach and running jump reach.
howTheDrillWorks:
Measure each player’s standing reach with feet flat.
The player completes two practice jumps.
The player performs three standing vertical jumps.
Record the highest valid reach.
The player then completes three running jumps from a standard five-metre approach.
Record the highest running-jump reach.
Calculate standing-jump height and additional reach gained from the running approach.
Record take-off leg, arm used and landing quality.
