Repeat any attempt affected by equipment movement.
Stop testing if landing control deteriorates.
coachingPoints: Measure standing reach accurately.
Require the same approach distance.
Record reach rather than relying only on device-generated jump height.
Observe landing mechanics.
Allow full recovery.
Do not permit contact with walls or equipment that alters the result.
Use a football target for role-specific interpretation.
Modify maximal jumping volume for younger and masters players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Difference between standing and running performance.
progressions: Add a football mark at maximum reach.
Test jumps from both take-off legs.
Use video to assess take-off and landing.
regressions: Replace maximal jumping with technique observation.
successIndicators: Reach effectively at the highest point.
matchApplication: Aerial reach affects marking, spoiling and ruck contests. Measuring reach and movement quality helps distinguish jumping capacity from ball judgement, positioning and contested technique.

title: Movement-to-Disposal Efficiency Test
objective: Measure how effectively each player converts high-speed movement into a balanced, accurate football disposal from multiple approach directions.
groundSize: A 35 × 30 metre testing area.
setup:
Place a central receiving cone.
Mark three approach lanes: straight, left-to-right and right-to-left.
Position a kicking target twenty metres away.
Position a handball target eight metres away.
Use a colour cue to determine the required disposal.
Establish a release-time limit after possession.
Prepare separate recording categories for movement time, balance, decision, accuracy and release speed.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins at the end of the nominated approach lane.
On the signal, the player accelerates towards the central cone.
A feeder delivers the football as the player enters the receiving area.
The coach displays a cue identifying kick or handball.
The player controls momentum, selects the required disposal and executes within the time limit.
Each player completes four repetitions from every approach lane.
Award two points for correct decision and accurate disposal, one point for correct decision but inaccurate execution, and zero points for the wrong disposal.
Record whether the player remained balanced.
Record release time and directional miss.
Calculate performance by disposal type and approach direction.
coachingPoints: Standardise feed timing and position.
Record balance separately from accuracy.
Use unpredictable disposal cues.
Avoid allowing players to slow before the receiving zone.
Compare approach directions.
Apply the same release-time limit.
Do not provide technical coaching during scored attempts.
Ensure kicking targets remain stationary.
progressions: Add multiple targets for option selection.
regressions: Use hand feeds rather than moving feeds.
successIndicators: Perform effectively from different movement angles.
matchApplication: Players rarely dispose from a stationary position. They must receive while moving, control momentum, recognise options and execute. This test identifies movement directions and disposal types that cause technical breakdown.

title: Repeat High-Intensity Effort Recovery Test
objective: Measure each player’s ability to recover between repeated high-intensity football actions while maintaining running output, clean possession and disposal quality.
groundSize: A 40 × 20 metre testing area.
setup:
Mark a starting line and a fifteen-metre contest cone.
Place a football beside the contest cone.
Position a handball target five metres beyond the starting line.
Mark a five-metre defensive recovery gate to one side.
Establish a fixed twenty-five-second recovery period between efforts.
Prepare recording columns for sprint time, collection, disposal, recovery movement and performance decline.
Assign one timer, one recorder and one football resetter.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player begins behind the starting line.
On the signal, the player sprints fifteen metres and collects the football.
The player turns and carries the football back towards the starting line.
Before reaching the line, the player handballs through the target gate.
The player then changes direction and accelerates through the defensive recovery gate.
Timing begins on the start signal and ends when the player crosses the recovery gate.
The player receives twenty-five seconds of recovery.
The sequence is repeated eight times.
Record every repetition time, collection result, handball result and recovery-gate completion.
Calculate fastest time, average time and percentage decline from the best to the final efforts.
coachingPoints: Apply the same recovery period to every player.
Record each effort rather than only the total test time.
Separate movement decline from skill decline.
Require clean possession before the return run.
Keep the recovery-gate direction consistent within a test.
Stop testing if movement becomes unsafe.
Avoid conducting the test after heavy conditioning.
Modify repetition numbers for youth, masters and returning players.
progressions: Add a kick instead of a handball.
Use a moving football at the contest cone.
regressions: Use controlled rather than maximal speed.
successIndicators: Repeat high-intensity efforts with limited decline.
Preserve safe running and turning technique.
matchApplication: Players regularly complete an attacking action, dispose of the football and then immediately recover into a defensive role. This test measures whether repeated effort and football quality can be maintained across a demanding sequence.

title: Position-Specific Running Pattern Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to complete the running and football actions commonly required in their nominated playing position.
groundSize: A half oval divided into defender, midfielder, wing and forward testing lanes.
setup:
Establish separate role patterns:
Defender: close, recover, receive and exit.
Midfielder: contest approach, spread, receive and dispose.
Wing: hold width, accelerate, receive and deliver.
Forward: lead, double back, mark and finish.
Mark every movement distance and disposal target.
Assign players to their current or proposed role.
Use the same pattern for all players tested in the same role.
Prepare role-specific scoring criteria.
Allow adequate recovery between attempts.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach explains and demonstrates the selected positional pattern.
The player completes one walk-through and two practice repetitions.
On the signal, the player completes the prescribed running sequence.
A feeder introduces the football at the nominated point.
The player completes the required role-specific disposal or scoring action.
Timing begins on the first movement and ends when the final action is completed.
Record movement time, route accuracy, football execution and recovery position.
Each player completes three valid repetitions in their primary role.
Suitable players complete two repetitions in a secondary role.
Compare results only with players completing the same positional pattern.
coachingPoints: Keep role patterns realistic rather than creating generic cone running.
Measure movement and football execution separately.
Require the player to follow the marked route.
Consider role purpose when interpreting speed.
Do not compare unlike positional patterns directly.
Observe whether the player understands when to accelerate and when to hold position.
Record communication where a teammate is involved.
Modify distances for age and competition level.
progressions: Add a decision at the final disposal.
Add a passive or live opponent.
Include a turnover during the pattern.
Use match vision to design role-specific routes.
Compare training results with match-running data.
regressions: Walk through the pattern before testing.
Test one section of the route.
successIndicators: Finish in an effective support or defensive position.
matchApplication: Different positions require different running patterns. This assessment measures movement in the context of a player’s role rather than assuming that one general running test represents every position.

title: Change-of-Pace and Separation Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to use changes of pace, direction and body shape to create separation before receiving the football.
groundSize: A 30 × 20 metre leading channel.
setup:
Mark a starting box for the attacker and defender.
Place three possible lead gates: straight, left and right.
Position a kicker twenty-five metres away.
Begin with the defender one metre behind the attacker.
Establish controlled body-contact rules.
Mark the point at which the attacker creates clear separation.
Prepare scoring categories for movement deception, separation, timing and mark completion.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker and defender begin inside the starting box.
On the kicker’s movement, the attacker begins a lead.
The attacker may change speed and direction before selecting one of the lead gates.
The defender attempts to remain within spoiling distance.
The kicker delivers when the lead becomes available.
Award two points when the attacker creates at least two metres of separation and completes the mark.
Award one point when separation is created but the mark is dropped or the delivery is untestable.
Award zero points when the defender remains in effective contest position.
Each player completes six repetitions as attacker and six as defender.
Record separation distance, lead timing, mark result and movement method.
coachingPoints: Assess how separation is created, not only final sprint speed.
Use consistent defenders where practical.
Repeat clearly untestable kicks.
Observe body deception before acceleration.
Record whether the lead begins too early or too late.
Match opponents appropriately.
Prevent holding or illegal blocking.
Allow adequate recovery.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to maintain the running line.
progressions: Add a live decision by the kicker.
Add an immediate shot at goal.
Test repeated leads with short recovery.
regressions: Use hand feeds instead of kicks.
matchApplication: Forwards, wingers and midfielders must create separation rather than relying only on straight-line speed. Effective pace changes produce marking opportunities and improve the quality of the kicker’s decision.

title: Closing-Speed and Pressure Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to close space rapidly, reduce speed under control and apply effective disposal pressure without over-committing.
groundSize: A 25 × 15 metre defensive pressure lane.
setup:
Position the ball carrier at one end of the lane.
Position the defender ten metres away.
Place a disposal target fifteen metres beyond the ball carrier.
Mark a one-and-a-half-metre control zone around the ball carrier.
Restrict the defender to pressure, corralling or smothering actions without tackling.
Define a legal pressure result.
Prepare scoring criteria for close speed, control, pressure and recovery.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins stationary with the football.
On the signal, the defender accelerates towards the carrier.
The carrier may begin moving or prepare to dispose.
The defender must close space and enter the control zone without making illegal contact.
The carrier attempts to kick through the target gate.
Award the defender two points for forcing an inaccurate disposal or legal smother.
Award one point for closing under control and reducing the carrier’s available space.
Award zero points for over-running, losing balance or failing to affect the disposal.
Each defender completes six repetitions from varied starting angles.
Record closing time, body control and disposal-pressure outcome.
coachingPoints: Reward control rather than reckless speed.
Observe the defender’s final three steps.
Require hands and body position appropriate to the disposal threat.
Do not allow front-on contact into a kicking player.
Vary approach angles.
Use consistent ball carriers.
Record whether the defender can remain involved after the disposal.
Provide recovery between maximal approaches.
progressions: Add a handball or sidestep choice.
Begin the carrier on the move.
regressions: Conduct the test at submaximal speed.
successIndicators: Maintain control in the final approach.
Recover into the next defensive action.
matchApplication: Effective pressure requires defenders to arrive quickly without running past the contest or conceding an easy evasion. This test identifies whether closing speed transfers into controlled and useful defensive pressure.

title: Contact Balance and Disposal Test
objective: Assess each player’s ability to remain balanced, protect possession and complete an effective disposal after controlled legal body contact.
groundSize: A 20 × 15 metre controlled-contact area.
setup:
Mark a five-metre approach lane.
Place a football at the centre of the lane.
Position a coach or player with a bump pad beside the collection point.
Place a handball target eight metres away and a kicking target twenty metres away.
Establish legal contact direction and force.
Match live opponents by size and experience where used.
Prepare ratings for collection, balance, protection and disposal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player accelerates towards the football.
The player collects the football while receiving controlled side contact from the pad.
The coach calls either handball or kick.
The player regains balance and completes the required disposal.
Each player completes five repetitions from contact on the left and five from the right.
Award one point each for clean collection, retained balance, secure possession and accurate disposal.
Record whether the player needs unnecessary recovery steps.
Advanced players repeat selected attempts against a controlled live opponent.
Rotate players through testing, feeding, contact and recording roles.
Stop the test if contact control or technique deteriorates.
coachingPoints: Use controlled, legal side contact.
Do not apply contact to the head, back or knees.
Assess balance rather than collision strength.
Require the player to protect the football.
Record both contact sides.
Separate possession retention from disposal execution.
Pair live opponents appropriately.
Avoid excessive repetition.
progressions: Add a live legal tackler after the initial contact.
matchApplication: Players frequently collect and dispose while absorbing bumps, tackles and body pressure. This assessment identifies whether contact disrupts balance, possession security or disposal quality.

title: Fatigue-Related Kicking Accuracy Test
objective: Measure how much each player’s kicking accuracy and technical consistency change after a standardised football-specific running effort.
groundSize: A 45 × 25 metre testing area.
setup:
Mark a twenty-metre kicking station with a four-metre-wide target gate.
Mark a repeated-running course consisting of three fifteen-metre shuttles.
Position a feeder at the kicking cone.
Establish a baseline set of five kicks before fatigue.
Use the same target, footballs and kicking distance for all sets.
Prepare recording categories for result, miss direction and visible technical change.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player completes five baseline kicks from the marked position.
The player rests for two minutes.
On the signal, the player completes three fifteen-metre shuttles at high intensity.
The feeder immediately provides a football.
The player completes one kick through the target gate within five seconds.
The shuttle-and-kick sequence is repeated five times.
Record kick accuracy and miss direction after every running effort.
Record the player’s running time for each shuttle set.
Compare baseline accuracy with fatigued accuracy.
Calculate the percentage change and note repeated technical breakdowns.
coachingPoints: Establish a reliable fresh baseline first.
Use the same running volume before every kick.
Apply the same disposal-time limit.
Do not provide technical coaching during scored attempts.
Record miss direction rather than only success or failure.
Monitor players for unsafe fatigue.
Allow the test to end if movement or kicking technique becomes unsafe.
Modify running volume for younger or masters players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Change in miss pattern under fatigue.
regressions: Use controlled rather than maximal running.
successIndicators: Limit the reduction in kicking accuracy.
matchApplication: Many important kicks occur after repeated running or defensive effort. This test identifies whether fatigue affects a player’s ball drop, balance, contact and target accuracy.

title: Fatigue-Related Decision-Making Test
objective: Assess whether increasing physical fatigue changes each player’s scanning, option selection, disposal speed and turnover response.
groundSize: A 45 × 35 metre small-sided game area.
equipment: Two scoring gates at each end
setup:
Create two balanced teams.
Place two scoring gates at each end.
Prepare a standardised two-minute running block around the outside of the playing area.
Assign observers to specific players.
Use an observation grid covering scanning, choice, release time, execution and turnover response.
Establish controlled contact rules.
Prepare fresh and fatigued assessment periods.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a four-minute small-sided game while fresh.
Observers rate assigned players using the decision-making grid.
Players complete the standardised two-minute running block.
The game restarts immediately for another four-minute period.
Observers rate the same players using the same categories.
A second running block is completed.
Players complete a final four-minute game period.
Coaches do not provide tactical feedback during the assessment.
Compare fresh, moderately fatigued and highly fatigued ratings.
Record whether decision quality, execution or transition response declines first.
coachingPoints: Use identical game rules across all periods.
Rate decision quality separately from execution.
Observe behaviour before possession.
Apply the same fatigue block to all players.
Track individual players rather than only the football.
Record repeated patterns rather than isolated mistakes.
Stop the test if fatigue becomes unsafe.
Consider positional role when interpreting decisions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Difference between fresh and fatigued behaviour.
progressions: Use full tackling for suitable players.
Use video to compare fresh and fatigued decisions.
regressions: Give the possession team an extra player.
Complete two game periods rather than three.
successIndicators: Select options appropriate to pressure and field position.
matchApplication: Decision quality often deteriorates late in quarters and after repeated high-intensity efforts. This test helps identify whether fatigue affects awareness, selection, execution or transition behaviour.

title: Off-Ball Work-Rate Observation Assessment
objective: Assess the frequency, timing and effectiveness of each player’s off-ball movements during a structured game rather than judging work rate only by possession counts.
groundSize: A 60 × 45 metre game area divided into three zones.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Mark defensive, midfield and attacking zones.
Assign observers to two or three players each.
Prepare observation categories:
Support run.
Defensive recovery.
Space creation.
Repositioning after disposal.
Communication.
Role discipline.
Define what qualifies as an effective action.
Use standard football rules with controlled contact.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play four five-minute periods.
Players rotate through nominated roles between periods.
Observers record every effective off-ball action by assigned players.
Possession involvements are recorded separately.
An action counts only when it improves space, support, pressure or structure.
Observers also record missed opportunities to move.
No individual work-rate feedback is provided during scored periods.
At the end of each period, observers finalise notes before discussing the game.
Compare effective actions by role and period.
Review whether off-ball work changes as fatigue increases.
coachingPoints: Do not confuse total running with effective movement.
Observe players away from the football.
Consider role and field position.
Record timing as well as distance.
Note movements that create opportunities for teammates.
Track defensive and attacking work separately.
Use repeated periods.
Support ratings with specific examples.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to create width or depth.
progressions: Add live GPS or movement tracking.
matchApplication: Much of a player’s contribution occurs without possession. This assessment identifies players who create options, defend space, support teammates and maintain structure even when they do not receive the football.

title: Return-to-Training Football Readiness Screen
objective: Provide a staged football-specific screen to help qualified medical, rehabilitation and coaching staff determine whether a returning player is ready to resume modified or full football training.
groundSize: A 35 × 25 metre rehabilitation and testing area.
equipment: Rehabilitation equipment as directed by medical staff
physicalLoad: 2–4 – Low to High according to approved stage
setup:
Confirm medical or rehabilitation approval before testing.
Review the player’s current restrictions.
Prepare five progressive stages:
Low-speed movement.
Straight-line acceleration.
Deceleration and direction change.
Football collection and disposal.
Position-specific movement.
Establish stop criteria for pain, instability, altered movement or reduced confidence.
Record the player’s pre-test symptom and confidence rating.
Ensure qualified staff supervise the screen.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player reports current symptoms, confidence and restrictions.
The player completes low-speed running and basic football handling.
If symptom-free and approved, the player progresses to controlled accelerations.
The player completes planned deceleration and change-of-direction movements.
Football collections, handballs and short kicks are introduced.
The player completes a limited position-specific pattern.
Staff assess movement quality, symptoms and confidence after each stage.
Testing stops immediately if defined concerns appear.
The player completes a post-test symptom and confidence report.
Medical and coaching staff determine the next permitted training level.
coachingPoints: This screen does not replace medical clearance.
Progress only through approved stages.
Do not pressure a player to continue.
Compare movement with the player’s normal pattern and previous results.
Record symptoms before, during and after testing.
Assess confidence as well as physical completion.
Avoid contact until separately approved.
Communicate the outcome clearly to all relevant staff.
progressions: Progress to contact testing only after separate approval.
regressions: Return to rehabilitation exercises directed by medical staff.
successIndicators: Move with appropriate control and symmetry.
Meet criteria agreed by qualified staff.
matchApplication: A player must tolerate football-specific running, stopping, turning and skill execution before returning to normal training demands. This screen supports staged progression while keeping medical judgement central.

title: Physical and Football Performance Assessment Review
objective: Review the physical and football-specific assessments completed from TA-021 to TA-039 and convert the results into practical individual and squad development priorities.
players: Minimum: 1 Ideal: Full Squad Maximum: Multiple Squads
groundSize: Clubrooms, meeting room and optional 30 × 20 metre verification area.
equipment: Footballs and cones for verification activities
time: 45–90 minutes for coach review; 10–20 minutes per player for feedback
setup:
Collect all valid results from TA-021 to TA-039.
Separate standard, modified and invalid tests.
Group results into acceleration, speed, agility, deceleration, repeat effort, aerial capability, contact balance, fatigue response, off-ball movement and readiness.
Prepare role-specific comparison groups.
Review the player’s baseline profile and current football role.
Identify results requiring verification.
Prepare a clear player-facing summary.
howTheDrillWorks:
Coaches confirm that all data has been entered accurately.
Invalid and modified results are identified.
Each player’s current results are compared with their previous baseline.
Results are compared with appropriate age, role and squad benchmarks.
Physical measures are reviewed alongside football-skill outcomes.
Coaches identify one physical strength and one football-linked movement strength.
Coaches identify no more than two priority development areas.
A practical training action is assigned to each priority.
The player receives individual feedback and may add their own observations.
A review date is established.
Squad-wide patterns are used to guide future training design.
Updated findings are stored in the player record.
coachingPoints: Do not create one overall physical ranking.
Compare players with their own previous results first.
Use role-appropriate benchmarks.
Interpret physical speed alongside football execution.
Consider injury history and test modifications.
Confirm unusual results before acting on them.
Limit the number of development priorities.
Use clear language in player feedback.
Protect confidential information.
Convert every priority into a training action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Differences between physical and football-specific results.
Speed loss when carrying or disposing.
progressions: Add video examples to player feedback.
Review whether training interventions improve later results.
regressions: Review three to five key measures.
Compare only with the player’s own baseline.
Use a simple written feedback form.
Delay benchmarking until sufficient data exists.
successIndicators: Understand one or two development priorities.
Recognise how results connect to their playing role.
Know when progress will be reviewed.
Use accurate and appropriately grouped data.
Interpret physical and football performance together.
Adjust training based on the findings.
matchApplication: Physical testing is valuable only when it explains or improves football performance. This review connects acceleration, agility, repeat effort, fatigue response, contact balance and off-ball movement to each player’s match role and future training plan.

title: Match Involvement and Action Coding Assessment
objective: Develop an objective record of each player’s match involvement by coding possessions, contests, support actions, defensive actions and transition behaviours during structured match simulation.
groundSize: Half to full oval according to player numbers.
setup:
Create two balanced teams and assign normal playing positions.
Prepare a coding sheet containing:
Possession won.
Effective disposal.
Ineffective disposal.
Contested involvement.
Support action.
Defensive pressure action.
Intercept or spoil.
Turnover response.
Role error.
Assign each observer no more than three players.
Ensure player numbers are clearly visible.
Establish the definitions for every coded action before play begins.
Use video as a secondary verification source where available.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a structured match simulation consisting of four periods of eight to twelve minutes.
Observers track assigned players rather than following only the football.
Every defined action is coded using the approved symbols or digital fields.
Possessions are recorded as contested or uncontested.
Disposals are recorded as effective, neutral or ineffective.
Off-ball support, defensive running and pressure actions are recorded separately.
Observers note major role errors or missed involvement opportunities.
Players rotate positions only between periods so role context remains clear.
Coding sheets are checked immediately after each period.
Video is reviewed where live observations are incomplete or disputed.
Results are reported as action frequencies, effectiveness rates and role-specific observations.
Coaches avoid reducing the assessment to total possession numbers alone.
coachingPoints: Define every coded action clearly before the assessment.
Track behaviour away from the football.
Separate action frequency from action quality.
Consider playing position and role.
Record missed opportunities only when the expected action was clearly available.
Avoid allowing one spectacular action to dominate the rating.
Use multiple periods to improve reliability.
Verify uncertain events through video where possible.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How often the player becomes involved.
Whether possessions are won in useful areas.
Work performed away from the football.
Whether the player performs the assigned role.
progressions: Add zone-based possession and pressure locations.
Track action chains leading to scores or turnovers.
Link coded actions with physical-running information.
regressions: Code three key action types only.
Assign one player to each observer.
Review recorded footage instead of coding live.
successIndicators: Contribute in actions relevant to their position.
Separate frequency, quality and role context.
matchApplication: Match contribution includes far more than possession totals. Coding contests, pressure, support, role execution and transition behaviour gives coaches a broader and more reliable picture of how a player influences the game.

title: Disposal Effectiveness Under Pressure Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to choose and execute an effective disposal while facing realistic closing pressure and restricted time.
groundSize: A 35 × 30 metre pressure-testing area.
setup:
Mark a central receiving zone.
Position one kicking target twenty metres away and two handball targets eight metres away.
Place a pressure player five metres behind the tested player.
Establish a maximum disposal time of three seconds after possession.
Use controlled closing pressure without tackling to ground.
Prepare separate scoring for option choice, disposal execution and turnover outcome.
Rotate pressure-player starting angles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The tested player begins inside the receiving zone.
A feeder delivers the football from the front or side.
As the football is released, the pressure player closes from behind or an angle.
The tested player scans and selects a kick, handball or short carry.
The disposal must be completed within three seconds.
Award two points for an appropriate and effective disposal.
Award one point for an appropriate option with inaccurate execution.
Award zero points for an unsuitable option, direct turnover or failure to dispose.
Each player completes twelve repetitions from varied pressure angles.
Record decision quality, release time, disposal type and outcome.
Repeat only feeds that prevent reasonable possession.
Rotate players through testing, pressure, target and recording roles.
coachingPoints: Apply pressure that is realistic but controlled.
Record the decision separately from execution.
Consider the direction and speed of pressure.
Avoid forcing one predetermined disposal.
Use the same release-time limit.
Record when the player protects the football effectively before releasing.
Do not coach during scored repetitions.
Match pressure players appropriately.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Body position between opponent and football.
matchApplication: Effective disposal in Australian football depends on pressure awareness, option selection and execution speed. This assessment identifies whether errors come from poor decisions, slow release, weak protection or technical breakdown.

title: Contested Possession Effectiveness Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to win, retain or neutralise possession in controlled one-on-one and small-number contests.
groundSize: A 25 × 20 metre contested-possession area.
setup:
Mark a central contest square five metres by five metres.
Place one exit gate on each side.
Pair players by size, age and experience.
Position a feeder outside the contest square.
Establish legal contact, tackling and release rules.
Prepare scoring for first possession, retained possession, effective exit and neutral result.
Assign qualified supervision to the contact area.
howTheDrillWorks:
Two players begin on opposite sides of the contest square.
The feeder rolls or bounces the football into the middle.
Players compete to win possession.
The possession winner attempts to exit through either gate with a legal disposal or controlled carry.
The opponent applies controlled legal pressure.
Award three points for winning possession and completing an effective exit.
Award two points for winning and retaining possession without an effective exit.
Award one point for neutralising the contest.
Award zero points for clearly losing possession and allowing an uncontested exit.
Each player completes eight one-on-one contests.
Advanced groups complete additional two-on-two contests.
Record first possession, control, disposal, pressure action and repeat effort.
coachingPoints: Match players appropriately.
Reward effective outcomes rather than first touch alone.
Record neutralisation as a legitimate result.
Require legal body contact and tackling.
Observe second and third efforts.
Use varied football entries.
Allow recovery between contests.
Stop the test if contact control deteriorates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Repeat effort after losing first possession.
progressions: Add immediate transition after the exit.
Begin with players in body contact.
regressions: Begin one player closer to the football.
Allow a handball to a stationary target.
matchApplication: Contested possession is not measured only by touching the football first. Players must secure, protect and release possession or prevent the opposition from achieving a clean exit.

title: Intercept Reading and Defensive Positioning Assessment
objective: Assess each defender’s ability to read play, position between the football and goal, intercept or spoil, and initiate a controlled defensive exit.
groundSize: A 50 × 40 metre defensive area.
setup:
Mark an attacking entry zone and a defensive intercept zone.
Place two attacking targets inside the defensive area.
Position two defenders between the targets and goal.
Place two defensive exit gates on the wings.
Assign a kicker and supporting attacking players outside the zone.
Prepare assessment categories for starting position, scanning, intercept decision, contest execution and exit.
Use controlled contact rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
Attackers circulate the football outside the entry zone.
Defenders adjust their position according to the football and attacking targets.
On the coach’s cue, the attackers deliver into the defensive area.
Defenders decide whether to intercept mark, spoil, cover the dangerous target or support a teammate.
If possession is won, defenders attempt to exit through a wing gate.
Play continues for six seconds after the initial contest.
Observers rate defender positioning before the kick, contest decision and exit action.
Each defensive pair completes eight to twelve entries.
Attackers vary the entry angle and target.
Defenders rotate roles and partners.
Clearly untestable entries are repeated.
Video may be used to review starting position and decision timing.
coachingPoints: Observe the defender before the kick is delivered.
Assess positioning relative to ball, opponent and goal.
Reward correct decisions even when execution is imperfect.
Distinguish intercept opportunities from situations requiring a spoil.
Record communication between defenders.
Continue assessment into the defensive exit.
Avoid predictable entry patterns.
Apply legal contest rules.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Movement as the football changes sides.
Decision to mark, spoil or hold position.
First disposal after possession is won.
progressions: Add live forward pressure after interception.
regressions: Use one attacker and one defender.
matchApplication: Intercept defenders must read play before the football is kicked. Positioning, judgement and communication determine whether they can attack the football without exposing dangerous space behind them.

title: Forward Involvement and Scoring Impact Assessment
objective: Assess each forward’s ability to create scoring opportunities through leading, contest work, possession use, finishing and defensive pressure.
groundSize: A full forward-50 area with an entry zone outside fifty metres.
setup:
Create an attacking team with three to five forwards.
Create a matched defensive unit.
Position additional players in the entry zone.
Establish normal football rules with controlled contact.
Prepare a forward-assessment sheet containing:
Effective lead.
Separation created.
Marking contest.
Ground-ball involvement.
Score assist.
Shot at goal.
Forward-pressure action.
Defensive role error.
Assign observers to individual forwards.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the entry zone.
Forwards organise and create leading or contest patterns.
The attacking team attempts to enter the forward line and score.
Play continues until a score, turnover or defensive exit.
Observers code assigned forwards throughout the full phase.
Forwards receive credit for effective movement even when they are not used.
Shot quality, scoring outcome and score assists are recorded separately.
Forward-pressure actions after turnovers are coded.
Complete four blocks of six to eight forward entries.
Rotate forward roles and starting positions between blocks.
Defenders provide realistic but controlled opposition.
Review output by role rather than possessions alone.
coachingPoints: Record effective leads that create space for teammates.
Separate opportunity creation from final scoring result.
Assess forward pressure after turnovers.
Consider the player’s assigned role.
Avoid judging deep forwards and high forwards by identical measures.
Use repeated entries from different angles.
Continue each repetition through the defensive exit.
Record shot difficulty and location.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to create or clear space.
progressions: Add repeated forward entries without full reset.
regressions: Use numerical advantage for the attacking team.
Assess one forward behaviour at a time.
successIndicators: Compete in marking and ground-ball situations.
matchApplication: Forward effectiveness includes creating space, competing, assisting scores, converting opportunities and preventing easy defensive exits. Goals alone do not fully represent a forward’s contribution.

title: Communication and On-Field Leadership Assessment
objective: Assess the clarity, timing, relevance and impact of each player’s communication and leadership behaviours during football activities.
groundSize: A 45 × 35 metre game area.
equipment: Video and audio recording where appropriate
setup:
Create two balanced teams.
Prepare communication categories:
Early information.
Directional call.
Defensive organisation.
Support or encouragement.
Role clarification.
Calm response after error.
Tactical adjustment.
Assign observers to specific players.
Explain that volume alone does not equal effective communication.
Use a game containing multiple options and turnovers.
Protect the privacy of any recorded audio.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete four five-minute game periods.
Observers record communication from assigned players.
Each communication action is classified by type and usefulness.
Calls are rated for timing, clarity and relevance.
Observers record whether teammates respond to the information.
Negative, distracting or late communication is recorded separately.
Players rotate formal leadership responsibility between periods.
Coaches provide no individual communication feedback during scored periods.
Results are compared across leadership and non-leadership periods.
Players complete a brief self-reflection after the activity.
Coaches compare self-perception with observed behaviour.
Feedback focuses on specific communication actions.
coachingPoints: Rate usefulness rather than loudness.
Record communication before, during and after possession.
Include non-verbal organisation where visible.
Assess emotional control after mistakes.
Consider whether teammates understand and use the information.
Avoid personality labels.
Provide quieter players with clear behavioural targets.
Use repeated periods.
progressions: Assign tactical changes for leaders to communicate.
Compare communication in fresh and fatigued states.
Review selected video or audio examples.
regressions: Allow coaches to pause between phases.
successIndicators: Adapt communication to the match situation.
matchApplication: Effective teams communicate before problems occur. Clear calls improve positioning, disposal decisions, defensive organisation, stoppage roles and transition response.

title: Player Self-Rating and Coach-Rating Alignment Review
objective: Compare player self-ratings with coach ratings to identify accurate self-awareness, confidence gaps and differences requiring evidence-based discussion.
players: Minimum: 1 Ideal: Full Squad Maximum: Multiple Squads
groundSize: Clubrooms or meeting area.
setup:
Select six to ten clearly defined performance categories.
Provide identical category definitions to players and coaches.
Use a controlled rating scale of one to five.
Require both parties to complete ratings independently.
Collect relevant testing and match evidence.
Identify categories where ratings differ by two or more points.
Prepare a private and constructive feedback environment.
howTheDrillWorks:
The player independently rates their current performance.
The coach independently rates the same categories.
Both identify one example supporting each high or low rating.
Ratings are placed side by side.
Areas of close agreement are acknowledged.
Differences of two or more points are discussed using evidence.
The player explains their interpretation before the coach responds.
Testing, training and match observations are reviewed.
The player and coach agree on a working rating where possible.
One strength and one development priority are selected.
A practical action and review date are recorded.
The completed review is stored confidentially.
coachingPoints: Complete ratings independently.
Use behaviour definitions rather than general labels.
Ask the player to explain first.
Use evidence from several sources.
Avoid using the process to win an argument.
Recognise that confidence and performance are different.
Protect privacy.
Finish with practical actions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether evidence changes the player’s view.
progressions: Compare ratings at multiple seasonal points.
Link ratings with individual development plans.
regressions: Discuss one strength and one priority.
Use simple examples for younger players.
Complete the process with parent or guardian support where appropriate.
matchApplication: Players improve more effectively when they understand their performance accurately. Alignment between player and coach reduces confusion, improves role clarity and creates more meaningful development goals.

title: Video-Based Performance Review Assessment
objective: Use selected video evidence to assess player decisions, movement, execution and role performance without relying solely on memory or possession statistics.
players: Minimum: 1 Ideal: 1–8 per review group Maximum: Full Squad across separate groups
groundSize: Meeting room or clubrooms with video display.
time: 20–40 minutes per player or position group
setup:
Select six to twelve clips for the player or group.
Include successful actions, errors and off-ball phases.
Organise clips by performance theme.
Prepare review questions covering:
Information available.
Options.
Decision.
Execution.
Movement after the action.
Ensure video is stored and shown according to privacy requirements.
Avoid selecting only extreme positive or negative moments.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach explains the purpose of the review.
The first clip is shown without commentary.
The player describes what they saw and intended.
The clip is replayed from available angles.
The player identifies available options and likely consequences.
The coach adds observations and role expectations.
The action is classified as effective, understandable but poorly executed, or requiring a different decision.
Off-ball movement before and after the action is reviewed.
The process is repeated across all selected clips.
Repeated patterns are identified.
One strength and one development priority are agreed.
A training action is assigned and documented.
coachingPoints: Ask the player to interpret the clip first.
Review the information available at the time.
Avoid judging with knowledge gained after the event.
Include off-ball footage.
Use repeated examples before identifying a pattern.
Separate decision and execution.
Keep feedback specific.
Limit the number of priorities.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ability to propose an improved action.
progressions: Allow the player to select clips.
Compare clips before and after an intervention.
regressions: Use training footage with clearer angles.
successIndicators: Accept and contribute to practical development actions.
matchApplication: Video allows players and coaches to review positioning, decisions and actions that are difficult to remember accurately. It provides evidence for targeted development rather than relying on general impressions.

title: Benchmark and Percentile Interpretation Exercise
objective: Teach coaches to interpret player benchmarks and percentile results accurately without treating rankings as permanent or complete measures of football ability.
players: Minimum: 1 Ideal: Full Squad data set Maximum: Multiple Squads
groundSize: Clubrooms, office or coach meeting area.
setup:
Select a valid testing data set.
Confirm that all tests used the same protocol.
Separate players by appropriate age, competition level and role.
Calculate squad average, median, range and percentile position.
Identify modified or incomplete results.
Prepare examples showing how the same raw score may have different meaning across roles.
Establish privacy rules for presenting rankings.
howTheDrillWorks:
Coaches review the definition of each test.
Raw scores are checked for errors and protocol differences.
The group calculates basic benchmark values.
Each player’s result is placed within the appropriate comparison group.
Coaches interpret percentile position without labelling it as a percentage score.
The group discusses the football relevance of each measure.
Results are compared with the player’s own previous performance.
Modified, injured or role-specific cases are considered separately.
Coaches identify which benchmarks are suitable for player feedback.
Coaches prepare a plain-language explanation of one selected result.
Development targets are based on realistic improvement rather than arbitrary ranking.
Benchmark definitions and limitations are recorded.
coachingPoints: Compare like with like.
Preserve raw scores.
Explain that a percentile describes relative position, not skill quality by itself.
Use sufficiently large and relevant comparison groups.
Consider test reliability and conditions.
Compare personal progress before squad ranking.
Avoid publishing sensitive rankings unnecessarily.
Connect every benchmark with football relevance.
progressions: Create age- and role-specific reference ranges.
Review whether benchmarks predict useful football outcomes.
regressions: Compare players with their own previous score.
Use category bands such as developing, expected and advanced.
matchApplication: Benchmarks can help identify strengths and development needs, but they must be interpreted in context. Football performance cannot be understood from ranking tables without considering role, decision making, skill execution and match behaviour.

title: Integrated Match Performance Assessment Battery
objective: Complete an integrated match-performance assessment combining live observation, action coding, role ratings, video evidence and player reflection.
groundSize: Half to full oval according to squad size.
setup:
Create two balanced teams.
Assign each player a defined role.
Prepare assessment responsibilities:
Match action coding.
Decision-making observation.
Contested-possession assessment.
Defensive or forward role assessment.
Communication and off-ball observation.
Assign manageable player groups to observers.
Set up video from suitable angles.
Conduct an assessor-calibration briefing.
Prepare a post-session player self-reflection.
Apply age-, competition- and contact-appropriate rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standard match-preparation warm-up.
Coaches explain the assessment format without revealing detailed scoring triggers that may distort behaviour.
Teams play four periods of ten to fifteen minutes.
Observers code their assigned performance categories.
Players remain in the same primary role for at least two periods.
Position changes are recorded clearly.
Video captures the full playing area where possible.
Coaches provide only essential safety and structural instructions during scored play.
Players complete a brief self-assessment after the simulation.
Observers check and finalise live records.
Selected video is reviewed to confirm key actions.
Results are entered into the player assessment system.
Each player receives a profile covering role execution, effective actions, development priorities and supporting evidence.
Squad-wide findings are used to guide future training.
coachingPoints: Calibrate observers before play.
Do not ask one coach to assess too many behaviours.
Separate action frequency, action quality and role execution.
Use video to verify rather than replace live observation.
Consider field position and game context.
Include off-ball and transition behaviour.
Apply consistent contact and safety rules.
Avoid one combined overall score.
Compare results with previous evidence.
Limit individual priorities to meaningful actions.
progressions: Link coded actions with running data.
Compare pre-season and in-season match profiles.
regressions: Assign one player to each observer.
Complete video review only for key uncertain actions.
successIndicators: Perform actions relevant to their role.
Demonstrate identifiable strengths and development needs.
Collect reliable live and video evidence.
Convert findings into clear training priorities.
matchApplication: The integrated battery provides a complete assessment of how a player performs within actual football phases. It combines skills, contests, decisions, movement, communication and role execution rather than relying on isolated tests or possession statistics.

title: Tactical Role Compliance and Adaptability Assessment
objective: Assess each player’s ability to understand, maintain and adapt their assigned tactical role across changing match situations without abandoning team structure.
groundSize: Half to full oval according to player numbers and tactical roles being assessed.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Assign every player a clearly defined tactical role.
Examples include defensive interceptor, accountable defender, inside midfielder, outside release, high forward, deep forward, defensive winger and stoppage sweeper.
Give each player a brief role card containing starting position, primary responsibility, support responsibility and turnover action.
Prepare three tactical conditions that will be introduced during play.
Assign observers to individual players or positional lines.
Establish assessment categories for positioning, role action, communication, adaptability and team connection.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin with an eight-minute match-simulation period under the original tactical structure.
Observers record whether assigned players begin in and repeatedly recover to their required positions.
Coaches introduce a tactical change between periods, such as a higher defensive press, an extra player behind the football or a deeper forward structure.
Players are given one minute to receive and clarify the adjustment.
A second eight-minute period is played under the new structure.
During the third period, the coach introduces a live tactical cue without stopping play.
Players must recognise the cue, communicate the change and adapt their roles.
Observers rate role understanding, positioning, execution, communication and response after turnovers.
Players complete at least one period in their primary role and one period in a related secondary role.
Ratings are supported with specific examples rather than general impressions.
Video is reviewed where available to confirm starting positions and structural decisions.
Players complete a brief role reflection after the activity.
coachingPoints: Define every role through observable actions.
Assess whether the player performs the role rather than whether they accumulate possessions.
Observe positioning before the football enters the area.
Record whether players communicate tactical changes to teammates.
Distinguish disciplined positioning from passive involvement.
Consider whether adaptation preserves overall team balance.
Assess attack-to-defence and defence-to-attack role changes.
Avoid changing tactical instructions too frequently for reliable observation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Position relative to teammates, opponents and the football.
Execution of the primary role responsibility.
Support actions when the football is elsewhere.
Recovery to role after possession changes.
Whether adaptation improves or damages team balance.
progressions: Allow captains to initiate the tactical change.
Introduce opposition tactical changes that must be recognised.
Assess players in multiple related roles.
Compare live observations with match video.
regressions: Walk through each role before play.
Introduce tactical changes only between periods.
Assess one role responsibility at a time.
Provide an on-field coach to support younger players.
successIndicators: Begin in the correct tactical position.
Perform the primary responsibility of the role.
matchApplication: Team systems depend on players understanding both their own role and how it connects with teammates. This assessment identifies players who can maintain structure, respond to tactical changes and contribute without being drawn unnecessarily towards the football.

title: Score-and-Time Scenario Decision Assessment
objective: Assess how effectively players adjust decisions, positioning and risk according to the score, remaining time and field position.
groundSize: Half to full oval.
setup:
Create two balanced teams.
Prepare at least six scoreboard scenarios.
Include situations such as:
Leading by four points with two minutes remaining.
Trailing by five points with ninety seconds remaining.
Scores level with forty-five seconds remaining.
Leading by one point with a defensive kick-in.
Trailing by two goals midway through the final period.
Protecting a lead with one player temporarily unavailable.
Assign observers to individual players or positional lines.
Define assessment categories for awareness, option selection, urgency, communication and tactical discipline.
Display the score and remaining time clearly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the first score, time and starting field position.
Play begins from the nominated restart.
Teams attempt to achieve the appropriate match outcome.
The countdown clock runs continuously.
Observers record player decisions in relation to the scenario.
The repetition ends when time expires, a decisive score occurs or possession leaves the defined area.
Teams receive thirty to sixty seconds to reset.
A new scenario begins from a different field position.
Players are not told the preferred solution.
Captains may communicate tactical instructions during play.
Each team completes attacking, defending and neutral-score scenarios.
Coaches compare decisions across several situations before assigning ratings.
coachingPoints: Ensure players know the score and time before every repetition.
Assess decisions according to the scenario rather than in isolation.
Observe players away from the football.
Record whether leaders communicate useful time information.
Distinguish appropriate urgency from rushed play.
Reward possession control when protecting a lead.
Reward direct attacking intent when time requires it.
Continue assessment after turnovers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Awareness of score and remaining time.
Whether disposal choices match the situation.
Positioning behind or ahead of the football.
Use of boundary, corridor and stoppage.
Ability to retain possession when appropriate.
Whether players recognise when a score is required immediately.
progressions: Hide the remaining time during the final thirty seconds.
Allow captains to call tactical changes.
regressions: Pause before play to discuss possible options.
successIndicators: Select risk appropriate to the situation.
Continue playing until the scenario is complete.
matchApplication: Close matches are often decided by awareness rather than isolated skill. This assessment identifies players who can recognise the scoreboard situation and adjust risk, urgency, positioning and communication accordingly.

title: Field-Zone Risk and Reward Assessment
objective: Assess whether players adjust disposal choice and risk according to their location in defensive 50, midfield and attacking 50.
groundSize: A 70 × 50 metre area divided into defensive, midfield and attacking zones.
setup:
Divide the ground into three field zones.
Create two teams with balanced numbers.
Mark a central corridor and two wider channels.
Establish normal football rules with controlled contact.
Use different scoring consequences by zone:
Defensive-zone turnover: three points to the opposition.
Midfield turnover: two points.
Attacking-zone turnover: one point.
Successful attacking corridor entry: two points.
Controlled defensive exit: two points.
Assign observers to players or positional lines.
Prepare assessment categories for scanning, risk, execution and turnover response.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins from a defensive restart.
The team in possession attempts to progress through all three zones and score.
Players may use the corridor or wider channels.
Turnover consequences are recorded according to the field zone.
Observers rate whether the disposal choice was appropriate for the player’s location.
After a turnover, play immediately changes direction.
The activity continues for four periods of five minutes.
Teams change ends after two periods.
Coaches do not prescribe a single disposal pathway.
Players rotate positions between periods.
Individual risk decisions are reviewed separately from skill execution.
Team patterns are assessed after the activity.
coachingPoints: Assess the location and consequence of each decision.
Separate a sound decision from poor execution.
Record whether players scan central and wide options.
Reward controlled exits from defensive 50.
Allow greater attacking risk where field position supports it.
Observe defensive positioning behind high-risk disposals.
Avoid creating a rule that permanently discourages corridor use.
Include turnover reaction in the assessment.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Choice of corridor, boundary or lateral option.
Risk level relative to field zone.
Whether repeated decisions match the player’s role.
progressions: Add kick-in and forward-entry starting phases.
regressions: Give the possession team an extra player.
Pause between phases for younger players.
matchApplication: The same disposal can be appropriate in attacking 50 and damaging in defensive 50. This assessment identifies whether players understand how field position changes the balance between attacking reward and turnover risk.

title: Kick-In Structure and Defensive Exit Assessment
objective: Assess the ability of the kicker and supporting players to organise, execute and adapt a structured defensive exit from a kick-in.
groundSize: Defensive 50 extending to the centre of the ground.
setup:
Create a defensive team and a pressing opposition team.
Mark three exit targets: short pocket, wide flank and central or opposite-side release.
Assign a designated kicker and defensive roles.
Give the defending team a controlled starting structure but do not prescribe every disposal.
Position opposition players in a realistic press.
Prepare assessment categories for setup speed, spacing, communication, kick selection, execution and second-phase support.
Establish a finishing line beyond defensive 50.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach signals a behind and places the football with the designated kicker.
Both teams organise from their nominated starting positions.
The kicker may play on or use the protected area according to normal rules.
The defensive team attempts to move the football beyond the finishing line under control.
The pressing team attempts to intercept and score.
Play continues until a controlled exit, turnover, stoppage or opposition score.
Complete six kick-ins with the same kicker.
Rotate the kicker and selected defensive roles.
Vary the opposition press between man-on-man, zone and high central pressure.
Observers record the kicker’s decision and the supporting movement.
Defenders receive credit for creating space even when they do not receive.
Results are reviewed by exit type and opposition press.
coachingPoints: Assess organisation before the kicker receives the football.
Record the quality of supporting leads and spacing.
Separate kick selection from execution.
Observe the second disposal after the kick-in.
Reward players who create width or clear dangerous space.
Vary the opposition press.
Continue the phase after the initial mark.
Assess turnover response inside defensive 50.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Selection of short, wide, central or switch options.
progressions: Add scoreboard pressure late in a match.
Require a switch after the first exit is denied.
Use full-ground transition after the exit.
regressions: Give the defensive team a numerical advantage.
Stop after the first successful disposal.
matchApplication: Kick-ins are structured opportunities to regain field position, but poor spacing or predictable decisions can create immediate opposition scores. This assessment reviews both the kicker and the connected defensive-exit system.

title: Full-Phase Transition Chain Assessment
objective: Assess whether players can connect defence, transition, forward entry and turnover response across a complete football phase.
groundSize: Full oval or a long three-quarter-ground area.
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams with full positional structure.
Begin each repetition from an opposition attack inside 50.
Assign observers to defensive, midfield and forward lines.
Prepare phase-assessment categories:
Defensive contest.
Possession win.
First exit.
Running support.
Midfield connection.
Forward entry.
Score creation.
Forward pressure.
Defensive reset after turnover.
Establish match-like contact and safety rules.
Use video where possible to capture the complete field.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession outside the opposition defensive 50.
The defending team attempts to win possession or force a turnover.
When possession changes, the defending team immediately attacks the opposite end.
Play continues through defensive exit, midfield transition and forward entry.
If the new attacking team scores, the repetition ends.
If possession turns over again, play continues until one team scores, exits cleanly or the time limit expires.
Each repetition lasts a maximum of forty-five seconds.
Teams reset to the original starting phase.
Complete eight to twelve full-phase repetitions.
Vary the initial attacking side and method of entry.
Observers score each phase separately and record where the chain breaks down.
Individual and unit results are reviewed after the activity.
coachingPoints: Assess every phase rather than only the final score.
Observe the first movement after possession changes.
Record whether players create width, depth and forward support.
Assess the balance behind the football.
Continue after secondary turnovers.
Identify the exact phase where structure or execution fails.
Use realistic time limits.
Provide sufficient recovery between high-intensity blocks.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: First disposal after possession is won.
Running support from behind and ahead.
progressions: Link observations with GPS or running data.
regressions: Provide the transitioning team with numerical advantage.
Stop after the first forward entry.
successIndicators: Secure and use the first disposal effectively.
Protect the ground behind attacking play.
matchApplication: Australian football is played through connected phases rather than isolated drills. This assessment identifies where a team’s transition chain succeeds or fails from defensive possession through to scoring opportunity and defensive reset.

title: Centre-Bounce Connection and Clearance Assessment
objective: Assess the ability of rucks, midfielders and connected players to execute centre-bounce roles and convert the initial contest into an effective clearance or defensive response.
groundSize: Centre square extending approximately forty metres in each direction.
setup:
Create two centre-bounce units with one ruck and nominated midfield roles.
Position connected wing, half-forward and half-back players outside the centre square.
Mark attacking and defensive exit gates.
Define legal contact and centre-bounce rules.
Prepare role-specific criteria for ruck, inside midfielder, defensive midfielder, outside release and connected players.
Assign observers to individual roles.
Use a consistent ball-up or throw-up process.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin in assigned centre-bounce positions.
The coach restarts play from the centre.
Teams compete to win the initial hit-out and clearance.
Play continues for eight to ten seconds after the first possession.
A successful attacking phase requires the football to pass through the attacking gate under control.
A defensive success includes winning possession, forcing a neutral stoppage or preventing a clean opposition exit.
Complete six centre bounces before changing selected roles.
Use varied ruck-hit plans and starting relationships.
Observers assess starting position, role execution, communication, contest action and post-clearance movement.
Ruck and midfield results are recorded separately and as a connected unit.
Complete at least two blocks against different opposition setups.
Video may be reviewed to confirm blocking and movement timing.
coachingPoints: Assess the connection between ruck and midfielders.
Record role execution rather than clearances alone.
Observe starting positions before the ball is in motion.
Include blocking, protection and defensive accountability.
Continue play beyond first possession.
Assess outside players who support the clearance.
Apply legal contact rules.
Avoid evaluating the ruck solely by total hit-outs.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Connection to players outside the square.
progressions: Add full forward and defensive structures.
Begin with an unexpected hit-zone call.
regressions: Use three midfielders without outside connections.
Stop after the first effective clearance.
successIndicators: Connect with players outside the contest.
Defend effectively after losing the clearance.
matchApplication: Centre bounces create immediate scoring and defensive consequences. This assessment measures the connection between the ruck, inside midfielders and surrounding structure rather than relying only on raw clearance totals.

title: Forward-Entry Quality and Retention Assessment
objective: Assess the quality of forward entries by measuring target advantage, possession retention, scoring opportunity and response when the entry is not marked.
groundSize: A forward-50 area plus a thirty-metre entry zone.
setup:
Create an attacking entry group, a forward unit and a defensive unit.
Mark left, central and right entry channels.
Assign forwards different roles, including deep target, high forward, leading forward and ground-level support.
Prepare entry-quality categories:
Direct teammate advantage.
Neutral contest.
Defender advantage.
Retained possession.
Shot created.
Score.
Forward-pressure outcome.
Assign observers to kickers and forwards.
Establish controlled contact rules.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking group begins with possession in the entry zone.
Forwards organise and move according to the available space.
The ball carrier selects and executes an inside-50 entry.
Play continues until a score, defensive exit or stoppage.
The entry is coded as teammate advantage, neutral or defender advantage.
Observers record whether the attacking team retains possession.
Shots, scores, score assists and forward-pressure actions are recorded.

title: Team Defensive Structure and Rotation Assessment

Opponent handover.
Rotation.
Intercept support.
Ground-level recovery.
Exit after possession is won.
Assign observers to defenders and the unit as a whole.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession outside defensive 50.
Attackers circulate the football before entering.
Defenders adjust their positions as the football changes sides.
The attack attempts to score.
Play continues until a score, defensive exit or stoppage.
Observers rate starting structure before the entry.

Complete four blocks of six attacking entries.
Vary the entry side, speed and attacking structure.
Rotate defensive roles between blocks.
Review individual actions and overall unit connection separately.

Record pressure on the ball carrier.

Use varied attacking patterns.

title: Testing and Assessment Chapter Final Assessment
objective: Complete a final integrated assessment that verifies player performance across technical, physical, tactical and match demands while evaluating the reliability and practical value of the club’s testing system.
groundSize: Full oval, half-oval testing stations and a private player-review area.
time: Two to three hours across one extended session or two separate sessions
setup:

Technical skill verification.
Football-specific physical and movement testing.

Integrated match-performance simulation.
Assign trained staff to every testing and observation responsibility.
Calibrate all coaches before testing.

Divide the squad into balanced testing groups.

Prepare video coverage and a central data-control point.
Ensure individual development plans and previous baseline results are available.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete a standardised warm-up.

Players complete role-appropriate movement assessments covering acceleration, agility, deceleration, repeat effort or aerial capability.
All raw results, test versions and modifications are recorded.
Players receive a recovery break.
The squad completes a tactical assessment covering role execution, field-position decisions or structured team phases.
Teams then complete an integrated match simulation.
Observers code possession quality, contested involvement, off-ball work, communication, transition and positional role execution.
Video is used to verify key actions and uncertain ratings.
Players complete a self-assessment after the practical session.
Coaches check all data before interpreting results.
Results are compared with previous baselines and appropriate role benchmarks.
Each player receives a review containing verified strengths and no more than two development priorities.
Individual development plans are updated.
Coaches review the reliability, efficiency and usefulness of every test used.
Tests that do not produce reliable or actionable information are modified or removed from future batteries.

Separate decision quality from execution.
Interpret physical results with football performance.

Avoid creating one overall player ranking.
Protect player privacy.
Convert every meaningful finding into a coaching or development action.

Whether any test creates unnecessary load or limited practical value.
progressions: Link testing with official match statistics and running data.

Use the complete system at pre-season, mid-season and post-season checkpoints.

Compare only with the player’s previous baseline.
